info.name: Kindlast
info.description:
The Kindlast HTTP surface, against the local compose stack (deploy/compose.yaml).

The collection is committed and reviewed alongside the code it describes, so it grows with the build order rather than drifting in one person's workspace.

**Two halves, with different futures.** The `auth` folder describes endpoints Zitadel serves and `web` redirects to. Those will never appear in a proto file, so this collection stays their source of truth. The `Core API v1` folder describes the proto surface, and once buf emits OpenAPI (design doc §23.2) those requests should be generated rather than hand-written, or the two will disagree.

**Requests marked NOT YET IMPLEMENTED** are here on purpose. They document the contract that the issue named in each description will deliver, so the collection tracks the plan rather than only the past.

No secrets live in this file. The client secret is generated by the seed job and belongs in a Postman environment or a vault, never in the repo.

variable.description: Zitadel. Published by compose on KINDLAST_AUTH_PORT, default 8300.
Caddy edge. Published on KINDLAST_EDGE_PORT, default 8000.

The console, through the Caddy edge (ENT-241). compose runs it as a container built from a production Next build, and it publishes no port of its own, so the edge is the only way in and the value is the same as edge_base_url. Point this at http://localhost:3000 instead when you are driving a development server started with `bun run dev`, which is the other console and stays supported: the seed registers an OAuth redirect URI for both.

core-api, through the Caddy edge (ENT-197). It still binds no published port of its own, so the edge is the only way in: the same door from the host as from another container, with no development-only shortcut. Paths are the Connect procedures, which are fully qualified proto names.

The web OIDC client, created by the seed job. Read it with:

docker run --rm -v kindlast_zitadel-machinekey:/k alpine cat /k/web-client.json
Seed-generated. Keep it in an environment, never in this file.
Set by the token request's test script.

A delegation credential (ENT-230). Minted by core-api while serving a signed-in person's own request and returned exactly once, so there is nothing to look up: the table stores only its SHA-256 digest. There is no mint endpoint yet, and the reason is in the delegated request's description. To try the path locally, mint one against the running stack:

docker exec -i kindlast-postgres-app psql -U kindlast_migrator -d kindlast -c "insert into act_delegations (id, org_id, user_id, acting_agent, token_hash, expires_at) values (gen_random_uuid(), 'a0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001', 'a0000000-0000-4000-8000-0000000000aa', 'analyst', encode(sha256('dev-delegation'), 'hex'), now() + interval '15 minutes')"

Then set this to `dev-delegation`. That insert is the migrator writing a row the application could only write for the person in its own session, which is the boundary being demonstrated rather than avoided.

item.description: The two checks that tell you whether the stack is actually up, and the ones CI runs.

request.description: Returns `ok`. The edge also routes `/kindlast.core.v1.*` to core-api as of ENT-197; web claims its own routes later in build-order step 1.

llama.cpp `llama-server`, the local model (ENT-235, §26.6). Returns 200 only once the weights are loaded, which is why the compose healthcheck uses it: a dependant waiting on this is waiting on a model that can answer, not on a process that has started.

No Authorization header, deliberately. Inference is local and the endpoint is bound to loopback, so there is no key to send. That is the point rather than an omission: a deployment holding a compliance record can run with no outbound internet at all.

The typed-output path §26.3 depends on. `llama-server` converts the JSON Schema to a GBNF grammar and constrains decoding, so the shape is guaranteed by the runtime rather than by the model choosing to comply.

THE TRAP, WHICH COSTS AN AFTERNOON IF YOU HIT IT BLIND: the schema constrains decoding and is NOT injected into the prompt. Notice the system message above describes the fields in words as well. Remove that description and you still get schema-valid JSON, with the wrong values in the right shape. Passing a Pydantic schema and assuming the model has seen it is the bug this request exists to demonstrate.

request.description:
The signing keys core-api verifies against, locally and cached, rather than introspecting per request (§1.4).

**This is `{"keys": []}` on a freshly seeded stack.** Zitadel generates a signing key lazily, on the first token it issues, so an empty set is correct rather than broken. It matters for ENT-195: a JWKS cache populated at boot would cache nothing and then reject every token, which is exactly why the acceptance criterion is that an unknown `kid` triggers a refetch.

exec: // Deliberately not asserting a non-empty set: see the description.
console.log('JWKS is empty, which is expected until the first token is issued.');

request.description:
A machine token, for exercising the API without a browser. The seed job creates the `core-api-client` service user this needs (ENT-195), so it works against any stack brought up with `docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml up -d`.

Fill `client_id`, `client_secret` and `project_id` from the shared volume rather than guessing:

```bash
docker run --rm -v kindlast_zitadel-machinekey:/k alpine cat /k/core-api-client.json
docker run --rm -v kindlast_zitadel-machinekey:/k alpine cat /k/core-api-audience.txt
```

Two details were measured against this stack rather than taken from a specification, and both cost an afternoon to rediscover.

**`client_id` is the service user's username, not its id.** The secret response carries its own `clientId`, and that is the one to send. Passing the numeric user id returns `invalid_client: client not found`.

**The audience is Zitadel's project id**, which is why the reserved scope `urn:zitadel:iam:org:project:id:{project}:aud` is in the scope list. Without it the token comes back scoped to the client itself, and core-api refuses it, correctly, as minted for someone else.

The scope story, which changed in ENT-197 and is worth reading before a `permission_denied` sends you looking in the wrong place. Zitadel's access tokens carry no `scope` and no `scp` claim whatever is requested here. With role assertion enabled they carry project roles under `urn:zitadel:iam:org:project:roles`, which `KINDLAST_OIDC_SCOPE_CLAIMS` points at, and that is what satisfies an endpoint declaring a real permission. `openid` is the exception: it is not a permission, nothing grants it, and verification asserts it, so an endpoint declaring it is reachable by any valid token. See `docs/core-api-configuration.md`.

The **user** flow is authorization code with PKCE and cannot be driven from Postman end to end, because it involves a login form and a redirect back to web. Use a browser for that.

exec: // The service user is seeded (ENT-195), so a failure here is a
// real failure rather than an expected gap, and is asserted.
// core-api accepts one audience and only one. If this fails, the
// reserved aud scope is missing or project_id is unset, and every
// core-api call will read as an audience mismatch.
// Recorded, not asserted: this is the known gap, and failing here
// would report a design decision as a defect.
console.log('No scope claim, as measured. core-api refuses this at the',
'scope stage until ENT-197 enables role assertion.');

request.description: The IdP's view of the subject. Note that core-api does not call this per request: it verifies the token locally (§1.4), so auth being down does not take the API down with it.

Revocation reaches the refresh token. Access tokens already issued stay valid until they expire, which is why sign-out also adds the `jti` to a Redis deny-list (§1.7). Without that second step, sign-out looks like it works and does not, for up to ten minutes.

request.description:
Builds the authorization URL with a PKCE verifier and state, then 302s. `?idp=google` adds an `idp_hint`.

Follow redirects off to see the 302 rather than the login page.
**POST with a CSRF token, never GET.** A GET logout can be triggered by a prefetch or an image tag, which signs the user out without them acting. ENT-197 asserts a GET is rejected.

item.name: Core API v1
item.description:
The proto surface, reachable from here as of ENT-197. core-api still binds no published port of its own, and CI asserts that absence rather than trusting it; the Caddy edge routes `/kindlast.core.v1.*` to it instead. That is the same door a container uses, which is the point: there is no development-only shortcut that stops existing in production.

These are Connect calls. Every one is a POST with a JSON body, including the ones that only read, and the path is the fully qualified proto name rather than a REST-style noun. An empty body is a parse error; the empty request message is `{}`.

The interceptor chain in front of these endpoints is live and tested as of ENT-195, and it is client-agnostic by construction: it verifies every token itself rather than trusting which door a request arrived through. `./scripts/validate-core-api-auth.sh` drives the whole chain and explains what each result proves.

One asymmetry to expect between this folder and a browser. The client-credentials token from the Auth folder is a machine token: it carries the project roles, so it passes endpoints declaring a real permission. A human token from the authorization-code flow cannot be obtained here at all, because that flow involves a login form and a redirect back to web. Use a browser for that, or `bun run --cwd apps/web test:e2e`, which drives it end to end.

Once buf emits OpenAPI (§23.2), these requests should be generated from it rather than maintained here by hand.

header.description:
The active organisation travels per request rather than in the token, so switching organisation needs no re-minting (§20.1).

Disable this header to exercise the bootstrap path: a caller who has never signed in has no organisation id to send, and the call has to work without one or a new user could never obtain one.

request.description:
The console bootstrap call: user, memberships with roles, active organisation, plan.

On a subject it has never seen it provisions a personal organisation and an owner membership in one transaction, idempotent on the `sub` claim. Required scope: `openid`, declared on the proto method.

**Answerable from here as of ENT-197**, now that the edge routes `/kindlast.core.v1.*` to core-api. It is a Connect call, so POST with a JSON body even though it reads: `{}` is the empty request message, and an empty body is a parse error rather than the same thing.

What `openid` means here is worth knowing before it surprises you. It is not a permission and no authorization server grants it: verification asserts it, so a token that passed signature, issuer, audience and expiry carries it whether or not the IdP said anything about scopes. Measured on this stack, a real Zitadel access token carries seven project roles and no `openid` at all. That is why this endpoint is reachable by a caller holding no grants, which it has to be, because this is where their first grant comes from.

Two behaviours worth knowing before you read a response. **The organisation header is optional on the first call** and must be: a client that has never signed in cannot know an organisation id, because none exists yet, so omitting it resolves the caller's default. And a brand-new organisation has no subscription row, so `plan` comes back `free` rather than empty.

How the personal organisation gets its name is worth knowing, because it involves a call you cannot see from here. It is named from the token's display name or email, and Zitadel puts neither in an **access** token, so core-api asks the provider's userinfo endpoint with your own access token and names it from that. Only on the request that provisions, never on later calls. If userinfo is unreachable or the provider declares none, the name falls back to the raw subject id, which looks like `386250729179840515` and is the symptom to recognise.

Each membership carries an `orgSlug` as of ENT-198, and that is what the console routes on: every authenticated page lives under `/o/{orgSlug}/`. It is derived from the name when the organisation is created and never recomputed, so it does not follow a rename. Use `orgName` for a label and `orgSlug` for a link; the two drift apart the moment anyone renames an organisation, and that is by design, because slugs live in bookmarks and in emailed approval links.

**`user` carries two identifiers as of ENT-220, and they are not interchangeable.** `user.id` is the IdP subject claim, a Zitadel snowflake like `386250729179840515`. `user.userId` is core-api's own key for the same human, a version 5 uuid derived from (issuer, subject), and it is what `memberships`, `created_by`, `approved_by` and **`Member.userId` from ListMembers** all store.

Compare `user.userId` when you want to know which row in a member list is the caller. Comparing `user.id` matches nothing and does so silently, which is the bug this field exists to close: before it, a console could list an organisation's members and not work out which one was the person reading the page, so an owner could not leave an organisation the API was perfectly willing to let them leave. The derivation is one-way, so you cannot compute one from the other client-side.

Creates an organisation and makes you its owner. **Implemented as of ENT-202.** Required scope: `org:manage`.

**No organisation header, deliberately.** This is one of two calls that carry none, the other being Accept invitation: in both you are establishing membership rather than exercising it, so there is no active organisation to name. Omit the header rather than sending it empty (§1.8) — an empty value is a client bug and should be refused, while its absence is a statement.

The slug is derived from the name by `org_slug()` at insert time and is immutable from then on. Send a name with umlauts to watch the transliteration: `Müller GmbH` becomes `mueller-gmbh`, not `m-ller-gmbh`. If the slug is already taken, the collision retry appends an ordinal and you get `acme-compliance-gmbh-2`, which is the correct answer rather than an error.

Copy the `orgId` from the response into the `org_id` environment variable to act inside the new organisation with the requests below.

Renames the organisation the header names. **Implemented as of ENT-202.** Required scope: `org:manage`, and owner-only on top of that.

**The slug does not follow the rename**, and the response returns it so you can see that rather than assume it. This is a product decision, not an oversight: slugs live in bookmarks and in emailed capability-token links, which are exactly the links a compliance product has to keep working. Rename a customer after an acquisition and every existing link still resolves.

Use `name` for a label and `slug` for a link. They drift apart the moment anyone renames, by design.

A member or viewer gets `permission_denied` rather than a call that appears to succeed and changes nothing.

Everyone in the organisation the header names. **Implemented as of ENT-202.** Required scope: `org:read`, not `org:manage` — seeing who your colleagues are is not an administrative act, and requiring the management scope would mean a viewer could not render a page they are entitled to see.

`displayName` and `email` are readable by every member regardless of role, which is a decision the product owner took explicitly on 2026-08-15 rather than a default nobody examined. Before that, `user_identities` was self-only and this endpoint could only have returned uuids. The reversal is narrow: it grants nothing outside a shared membership, and nothing outside the organisation the header names. See `db/migrations/00005_co_member_identity.sql`.

Both fields can be empty and a client must cope. `displayName` is absent when the authorization server returned no name claim, and both are absent for someone invited who has not yet signed in.

Copy a `userId` from the response into the `member_user_id` environment variable for the two requests below.

Changes one member's role. **Implemented as of ENT-202.** Required scope: `org:manage`, owner-only.

Three roles exist and no more: `owner`, `member`, `viewer`. Anything else answers `invalid_argument` naming the three, rather than letting the database's check constraint reply with `memberships_role_check`, which is a correct answer to the wrong audience.

**Demoting the last owner is refused** with `failed_precondition`, not only removing them. Guarding removal alone would be theatre: a last owner who cannot be removed could be demoted to viewer and then removed, reaching the same ownerless organisation in two steps. An organisation with no owner has nobody who can invite, change roles or manage billing, and no way back short of an operator opening a database session.

The response re-reads the member rather than echoing what was sent, so it describes what the database holds.

Removes someone from the organisation the header names. **Implemented as of ENT-202.** Required scope: `org:manage`, owner-only.

Removing the last owner answers `failed_precondition`; see Update member role for why that rule covers demotion too.

A user id that is not a member of this organisation answers `not_found`, and so does one that does not exist at all. That ambiguity is deliberate: distinguishing them would turn this endpoint into a way of asking whether a given person belongs to a given organisation.

Creates an invitation to the organisation the header names. **Implemented as of ENT-202.** Required scope: `org:manage`, owner-only. Invitations expire after seven days.

**The response does not contain the token, and never will.** It carries `invitationId` and `expiresAt` only. The raw token exists in exactly two places: the email sent to the invitee, and a SHA-256 hash stored against the row. Returning it here would let anyone who can invite also redeem on the invitee's behalf, which defeats the point of a capability sent to an address.

A practical consequence for anyone testing from here: you cannot chain this into Accept invitation. To exercise acceptance, write a fixture invitation with a token you already know, which is what the Go tests do via the store's `CreateInvitation`.

**Email delivery works as of ENT-219.** The invitation and the email carrying it are written in one transaction: the raw token exists only inside this handler, so a row committed without its message would be permanently undeliverable rather than merely unsent. The message lands in `transactional_outbox` and a dispatcher drains it onto SMTP, which on the local stack is Mailpit at `localhost:8025`. Expect it within about ten seconds, which is the dispatcher's interval.

**The queued message is redacted afterwards, as of ENT-242.** The body carries the accept link, and the accept link carries the raw token, so `transactional_outbox` is the one place in the schema holding a bearer credential in the clear. The dispatcher clears the address, subject and both bodies once the message can no longer be usefully sent: seven days after delivery, or sooner if the invitation is accepted or expires. The delivery fact stays. Two consequences for anyone testing from here. A message you sent last week has an empty body in the table and is still in Mailpit, which is where to read it. And an invitation that expired before its mail server came back is now moved to `failed` rather than retried forever.

**This can now answer `failed_precondition`,** and the message says so: a deployment with no `KINDLAST_APP_BASE_URL` refuses to invite rather than minting an invitation whose link cannot be built. That is not a caller error to retry. The alternative is worse than refusing, because the invitation would be stored, listed as pending, and impossible either to accept or to repair.

A deployment with no `KINDLAST_SMTP_ADDR` still accepts the call. The message queues as `pending` and delivers whenever SMTP is configured, which is the outbox working rather than failing.

Email validation is deliberately shallow: non-empty and containing an `@`. Anything stricter rejects addresses that are valid under RFC 5321, and the authoritative test of an address is whether mail to it arrives.

Ordering matters and is easy to get wrong: this must run **before** the first GetCurrentUser. Get it backwards and every invited user ends up owning a personal organisation they never asked for, alongside the one they were invited to. `web`'s callback enforces that ordering (ENT-197); a direct caller has to keep it themselves.

**Implemented as of ENT-196**, and reachable from here as of ENT-197. Required scope is `openid`, not `org:manage`: the caller is redeeming a capability they were sent and holds no role anywhere until it succeeds, so an organisation scope would make a first invitation impossible to accept.

**The caller must be the person the invitation names (00033).** Acceptance matches the invited address against the `email` claim on your token, case-insensitively, and the claim must be verified (`email_verified`). Holding the token is no longer sufficient on its own: an invitation sent to somebody else is refused, and refusing it does not consume it, so the intended recipient can still use it afterwards. A mismatch is reported exactly like expired, already accepted and never existed, a `not_found` reading `this invitation cannot be used`, so this endpoint cannot be used to discover which tokens are real or who they were for. If you are driving this by hand, mint your token for the address you invited or it will refuse.

The token is sent in the clear here and stored hashed, so the value in the database never matches this one. **Issuing invitations exists as of ENT-202** (see Invite member above), and that endpoint still deliberately never returns the token, so you cannot chain the two from the response alone.

On a local stack you no longer need a hand-written fixture though: as of ENT-219 the invitation email is actually delivered, so call Invite member, open Mailpit at `http://localhost:8025`, and copy the token out of the link in the message. That is the same path a real invitee takes, which makes it a better test than a fixture. The Go tests still write a known token directly, because they must not depend on a mail server.

Expired, already accepted and never existed all answer `not_found` alike, deliberately, so this cannot be used to discover which tokens are real.

The response carries `orgSlug` as of ENT-198, so a client can redirect straight into `/o/{orgSlug}/` rather than making a second call to find out where the organisation it just joined actually lives.

The feed: findings for the organisation the header names, newest first. Required scope: `findings:read`.

**Implemented as of ENT-203.**

**A signed-in human reaches this. The client-credentials token above does not, and that is correct rather than a gap.**

ENT-221 resolved in two parts. #134 granted the project roles, which the seed had been creating and giving to nobody. #135 went further: core-api now derives a human's scope set from the token's OAuth client rather than from granted roles, so every signed-in person holds the same fifteen scopes by construction. Verified in a browser, not inferred.

**Machine clients are deliberately unchanged.** They still read granted scopes, which is what keeps the scope layer a real boundary for them, and `core-api-client` holds only `internal:*`. So the token this collection mints answers `permission_denied` here, from the scope interceptor rather than from the handler. Measured, not assumed.

To exercise this request as-is you would have to grant the service user `findings:read` in Zitadel. That is deliberately not seeded: `internal:*` is the vocabulary a machine is meant to hold, and granting it human scopes would blur the one distinction the client-class mechanism exists to draw. Reaching it as a human means going through `web`.

Pagination is keyset, not offset, over the `(org_id, created_at desc)` index 00002 built for this query. `pageToken` is opaque: do not parse or construct one. Send `pageSize: 0` (or omit it) to let the server choose. Treat a non-empty `nextPageToken` as the only signal that more exist — a full last page is ordinary and would otherwise read as another page waiting.

`status` filters to one of `pending`, `approved`, `rejected`, `snoozed`. Omit it for every status, which is what the feed's default view wants: a finding somebody already dealt with is still part of the compliance record.

**Every finding carries `narrative`, `agentRunId` and `narrativeRefusal` as of ENT-162 and ENT-164.** They are what the Analyst added over `IntelligenceService.DraftNarrative`, and they sit beside the sweep's own columns rather than over them: `detected`, `proposedAction`, `severity` and the citation are exactly what they were before any run happened.

**Absent is the ordinary answer, not a gap.** Narration is a job that runs after the sweep (`NarrativeService.NarrateFindings`), Intelligence sits behind a compose profile, and a stack without that profile narrates nothing and is a supported deployment. Connect's JSON drops empty strings, so a finding nobody has narrated simply has none of these three fields.

**`narrative` is prose and `detected` is a heading. Do not swap them.** That is ENT-164, and it is a bug rather than a style note: the layer this replaces wrote model prose into `detected`, which the console renders as a card heading, so a short phrase became a three-line paragraph. A client renders `narrative` in the body.

**`narrativeRefusal` is set when a run was made and the guardrail ring rejected the draft**, usually because it cited an article the finding is not about. It never arrives alongside `narrative`. It is deliberately not rendered in the console's feed list, only on the single-finding page: a list where every row reports what our pipeline could not do is a list about us rather than about the customer's compliance.

**`citation.obligationSummary` IS THE AUTHORED STATEMENT OF THE LAW, AND IT IS THE FIELD TO RENDER BESIDE `narrative` (ENT-248).** Two live narrations on the 2B tier cited Article 30 correctly and stated Article 30(5) backwards in the prose beside the citation, which is a failure the customer who checks the citation cannot detect: they follow it, find it valid, and believe the sentence next to it. So the model no longer states the law at all, and the statement reaches the page from the corpus row instead.

Render it **verbatim**. Not truncated, not clamped, not summarised: a summary of the summary is a second author, and the product's whole claim is that a human can check what we say against the law. Same rule as `label`.

Unlike `label` and `url`, which are what the Analyst assembled when the finding was created and must never change under it, this is read live from `obligations`. That difference is deliberate: a curator correcting a statement of law should reach every finding citing it, because the alternative is a customer reading a sentence we already know to be wrong. Empty when the obligation has no summary, and a client then renders nothing rather than a placeholder.

One finding plus the quoted regulatory text behind it. Required scope: `findings:read`. **Implemented as of ENT-203, and reachable by a signed-in human as of ENT-221.** See List findings for why this collection's client-credentials token still is not the way to call it.

The `supporting` array comes from `finding_supporting_chunks`, which is org-gated in the database as well as in the handler and returns no rows rather than raising when the finding belongs to someone else.

**An empty `supporting` array is normal and is not an error.** The corpus does not cover every instrument an obligation can cite. Empty means "we cannot show you the text here", which is honest; it is not the same as the citation being absent, and a client renders the citation either way.

**On the `citation` object, which is the part worth reading carefully.** Every field in it is a value the database already stored, assembled by `analyst_citation_label` and `analyst_citation_url` when the finding was created. Render `label` and link `url`. Do **not** rebuild the label from `celex` and `article`: a second assembler is a second thing that can be wrong, and the product's whole value is that a human can check the claim against the law.

**On `narrative`, `agentRunId` and `narrativeRefusal`, which this response carries as of ENT-162 and ENT-164.** See List findings for what they are and why an absent one is ordinary. What is specific to this endpoint is that it serves the page a person opened about one finding, so it is where the console shows the narrative in full and where it shows a refusal at all.

**`agentRunId` names the `agent_runs` row that produced the narrative or the refusal, and it is a reference rather than a link.** `agent_runs` has a write path (`IngestService.RecordAgentRun`) and no read path yet, so nothing can resolve the id to a run: measured on 2026-08-18, not inferred. The console prints it, because an id somebody can quote in a support conversation is worth more than nothing, and a read RPC is proposed rather than smuggled in here.

The act path. Required scope: `findings:act`, which is deliberately **not** `findings:read`: rendering the console and approving on a human's behalf are separately dangerous, and a display-only integration should not be one credential leak away from the second.

**Implemented as of ENT-203**, database half included (`00006_act_path_audit.sql`, which is what makes the audit row exist at all). Reachable by a signed-in human as of ENT-221; see List findings for why this collection's client-credentials token still is not the way to call it.

**Plan gating.** With `KINDLAST_BILLING_ENABLED` set, an organisation not on an active `pro` subscription gets `resource_exhausted` here rather than `permission_denied`: the two mean different things to the person reading the console, and only one of them has a button under it. Unset, which is the self-hosted default, the act path is ungated (§18.1).

**There is no actor field, and there will not be one.** The approving human is read from the session GUC the tenancy interceptor set, so a caller cannot name someone else as the approver. `approve_finding` lost its acting-user parameter in the ENT-192 rewrite for exactly this reason.

**Idempotent.** Approving an already-approved finding returns `applied: false`, writes nothing and writes no second audit row. The usual cause is a double submit or a retry, neither of which is a problem worth showing a customer.

`applied: false` also covers a finding that is unknown or belongs to another organisation. All three answer alike on purpose — telling them apart is what probing for a tenancy leak looks like.

**`createdRecordId` is populated as of ENT-203, and which findings populate it is a data question rather than a code one.** 00007 gave obligations an `action_type` and made `analyst_convert_signal` copy it onto the finding; 00009 classified the three obligations where approving means something other than "a human read it". So approving a `gdpr-art-30-ropa` finding returns a `processing_activities` id, an Annex III or Article 26 finding returns an `ai_systems` id, and the other twelve obligations stay `review` and create nothing — which is the right outcome for an obligation whose remedy is not a row. Verified end to end through the console, not inferred from the migrations.

**No obligation maps to `create_dsar`, and 00009 asserts that rather than leaving it to chance:** a data-subject request arrives from a person, so an obligation that manufactured one would be inventing the requester.

`createdRecordId` is empty on a repeat approval even though the record exists, because nothing was created by that call. This field reports what this request did; `RecordsService` answers what is on file.

`reviewed` records whether a human actually read the supporting text rather than approving from the feed card. "Approved" and "approved having read the regulation" are different claims and the audit trail can tell them apart.

item.name: Approve finding, as an agent acting for a person

request.description:
The same RPC as above, called by an agent on a person's behalf. **Implemented as of ENT-230.** No new endpoint and no new scope on the request: what changes is who the request is for.

**`Kindlast-Delegation` is the whole of the difference, and it is a header rather than a field** because it applies to the request rather than to what the request is about. Every RPC on this surface honours it; none of them grew a field for it.

**The token here is the client-credentials one, and it needs `internal:act-on-behalf`.** That scope is issued to service principals and never to the browser client, so a console token cannot present a delegation at all. Note what it does NOT need: `findings:act`. The machine holds no human scope and never will.

**WHAT THE DELEGATION CHANGES, IN ORDER.**

1. **Scope.** The caller's own scopes are REPLACED by the set a signed-in person holds, not unioned with them. Union would give a delegated request the person's authority plus the platform surface, which is strictly more than either party has. So this request may approve a finding and may not reach `RecordAgentRun`, and the same token with no delegation header may do exactly the opposite.
2. **Tenancy.** Both session GUCs are set to the PERSON. From there down the request is indistinguishable from that person at the keyboard: the same policies, the same membership check, the same role gates in the handler. An agent acting for a viewer gets `permission_denied` from `InviteMember` for the identical reason the viewer does.
3. **Audit.** The row names the person as the actor, snapshots the role they held, and adds `acting_agent` naming what held the pen. "The Analyst, on behalf of Ada, at 14:02".

**`Kindlast-Org-Id` is deliberately absent.** A delegation is single-org and the header does not get a vote: send one naming a different organisation and the request is refused, even when the person is a member of both, which is exactly the consultant case. A header naming the delegation's own organisation is accepted, because a client that sets it uniformly is not making a claim.

**There is no mint endpoint in this collection, and that is the design rather than a gap.** A delegation can only be created from inside a transaction that is already the person's: the policy on `act_delegations` checks the row against the two tenancy GUCs, so a handler that read the user id out of a request would be refused by Postgres rather than obeyed. Nothing a machine can call could mint one, because any such endpoint would have to be told whose delegation to make, and being told is the thing this design exists to avoid. The rail mints one while serving the person's own request. See the `delegation` variable for how to make one by hand against the local stack.

**It expires, and it is revoked on the way out.** The TTL is minutes and the database refuses anything over an hour, for any writer including the migrator. Revocation is the fast path for a run that finishes cleanly; the ceiling is what holds when a run crashes instead. An expired, revoked or invented delegation all answer `permission_denied` with one message.

**Losing your membership stops your agent.** Membership is checked on every call rather than snapshotted at mint, so somebody removed at 14:05 does not keep acting until 14:20 through something they are no longer entitled to drive.

**The second consumer of this primitive now exists (ENT-249), and it cannot use this header.** §8's one-tap approve link is the same delegation bound to one finding, and `resolve_act_delegation` matches that binding symmetrically: a delegation with a finding is invisible to a caller naming none, so an approve link presented here resolves to nothing and answers `permission_denied` like any other unusable credential. It is spent through `POST /api/v1/approve` and nowhere else. The reverse holds too: the delegation in this request names no finding, so it cannot be spent through the approve endpoint.

Rejects a finding, optionally saying why. Required scope: `findings:act`. **Implemented as of ENT-203**, and reachable by a signed-in human as of ENT-221; see List findings for why this collection's own token is not.

**The reason is worth sending even though it is optional.** Three rejections of the same obligation on the same profile raise a `product_review_flags` row, carrying the distinct reasons given. That is the mechanism by which a bad rule gets noticed rather than being quietly dismissed by every customer in turn, and it only works if the reasons are there.

Idempotent in the same way as approve: rejecting an already-rejected finding returns `applied: false`, keeps the first reason, and writes no second audit row.

Defers a finding. Required scope: `findings:act`. **Implemented as of ENT-203**, and reachable by a signed-in human as of ENT-221; see List findings for why this collection's own token is not.

`days` is clamped to 1..365 by the database; `0` or an omitted value means the default of 7. A snoozed finding returns to `pending` when `expire_snoozed_findings()` next runs, which the `expire-snoozed-findings` Temporal Schedule does hourly as of ENT-256 (see Expire snoozes).

**Unlike approve and reject, this is deliberately not idempotent.** Snoozing an already-snoozed finding writes a second audit row, because deferring again is a second decision with a new date. A trail that recorded only the first would say a finding was deferred once when a human deferred it four times, which is precisely what an auditor is looking for.

Runs the Watcher and then the Analyst for the organisation the header names. **Implemented as of ENT-203.** Required scope: `internal:ingest`.

**This is the one request here the client-credentials token above is actually for.** Every other Core API request needs a human scope, which a machine client does not hold; this one needs `internal:ingest`, which is a machine scope and nothing else is meant to have.

**The seed grants it as of ENT-221**, so this works from here where the others do not. That asymmetry is the design rather than an accident: `internal:*` is issued to service users and never to a browser client, and the human scope set in core-api deliberately contains none of it.

**Why this endpoint still exists.** As of ENT-256 (part four) sweeps run on Temporal: confirming onboarding enqueues one (see List sweep triggers) and `sweep-every-organisation` runs daily at 06:00 UTC over every organisation with a profile. Both workflows call this surface as activities (Run sweep with `detectOnly: true`, then Run analyst), so this request is what the worker calls, kept for an operator who wants to sweep one organisation now and see the counts.

**It runs as a different database role.** `core-api` serves requests as `kindlast_app`, which deliberately cannot create findings: the thing exposed to the world should not be able to fabricate a claim about a customer's legal exposure. Sweeps run on a second pool as `kindlast_agent` (00008). If `KINDLAST_AGENT_DATABASE_URL` is unset the service is not served at all and this answers `unimplemented`, which is a supported configuration rather than a fault.

**Per-organisation, never global.** A request with no `Kindlast-Org-Id` is refused with `invalid_argument` rather than defaulting. Doing nothing would look like success, and sweeping everyone has every customer in its blast radius, so sweeping the estate is a loop somebody writes deliberately.

`detectOnly` runs the Watcher and skips the Analyst. Use it when the feed is empty and you need to know which half is quiet: the Watcher finding nothing wrong is a different failure from the Analyst failing to resolve an obligation.

`findings` lower than `signals` is normal, not an error. A signal whose obligation slug resolves to nothing is skipped and logged, because a finding with no obligation behind it could not cite anything.

Brings back every finding whose deferral has run out, across every organisation at once. **Served as of ENT-256 (part two).** Required scope: `internal:ingest`, the same machine scope as Run sweep, so use the client-credentials token.

**No `Kindlast-Org-Id` header, and that is the point.** A sweep names one organisation because sweeping everyone is a blast radius somebody should have to write a loop for. Expiring snoozes is the opposite: a maintenance pass whose whole job is every organisation, that decides nothing (the person decided when they deferred), and the database function behind it is `SECURITY DEFINER` and executable by the producer role alone (migration 00034). Sending the header changes nothing.

**You will not normally call this.** It is the activity behind the `expire-snoozed-findings` Temporal Schedule, which `workers` registers at boot and runs hourly. It is here so an operator can run a pass by hand and see the count, and because the collection documents every RPC on the internal surface. Idempotent: a second call in the same hour reports `reemerged: 0`.

The response carries `reemerged` (how many findings returned to needing a decision) and `ranAt` (the database clock inside the transaction, so it is the instant they actually moved).

Runs the Analyst alone for the organisation the header names: turns the signals the Watcher raised and nobody has analysed yet into findings. **Served as of ENT-256 (part four).** Required scope: `internal:ingest`, so use the client-credentials token. Refused with `invalid_argument` without `Kindlast-Org-Id`, for Run sweep's reason.

This is the second activity of every sweep workflow, after Run sweep with `detectOnly: true`: the design's point is that the Analyst is the next step in the workflow, not a second schedule five minutes later hoping the first finished, and part five puts the Python narrative step between them. Idempotent: the Analyst works over unprocessed signals, so a second call finds none and reports `findings: 0`.

Lists the sweeps somebody asked for and nothing has run yet: trigger id, organisation and reason, oldest first. **Served as of ENT-256 (part four).** Required scope: `internal:ingest`. No `Kindlast-Org-Id`: the list is every organisation's.

Confirming onboarding writes a `sweep_triggers` row (migration 00035) in the same transaction as the profile, so a row here cannot name a profile that is not yet visible. The `relay-sweep-triggers` Temporal Schedule asks this every fifteen seconds and starts one `sweep/{trigger id}` workflow per row. You will not normally call it; it is here so an operator can see what is waiting.

Records what a triggered sweep did. **Served as of ENT-256 (part four).** Required scope: `internal:ingest`. `OUTCOME_DONE` marks the row done; `OUTCOME_FAILED` with `error` records the attempt and the reason and leaves the row pending, so the relay offers it again once the workflow that held it has closed. Idempotent: a row already done answers `settled: false`.

Lists every organisation a scheduled sweep should visit: the ones with a compliance profile, by id alone. **Served as of ENT-256 (part four).** Required scope: `internal:ingest`.

**This is "sweep everyone", written deliberately.** Run sweep refuses to sweep more than one organisation because the blast radius is every customer at once; this RPC exists so that the loop is the `sweep-every-organisation` workflow, one organisation per activity pair, visible and pausable in the Temporal UI, rather than a parameter somebody can pass by accident. The producer role cannot enumerate tenants, so the answer comes from `sweep_targets()`, the ninth SECURITY DEFINER function (migration 00035), which returns ids and nothing else.

Lists what is waiting to leave core-api, oldest first, by row id only: `messageIds` for invitation emails in the transactional outbox and `notificationIds` for finding notifications (ENT-256, part three, second half). **Served as of ENT-256 (part three).** Required scope: `internal:ingest`, the machine scope, so use the client-credentials token. No `Kindlast-Org-Id` header: the outbox is every organisation's, and the worker that calls this holds no tenant.

**Ids and nothing else, on purpose.** This is the relay's question, asked every fifteen seconds by the `relay-transactional-outbox` Temporal Schedule, and its answer is written into a workflow history that is kept for the namespace's retention and readable in the UI. The address, the subject and the body (which for an invitation carries the raw bearer token in the clear, migration 00030) are read by Deliver message inside core-api and never cross that boundary.

`limit` bounds one call (default 200, at most 1000); what is not listed now is listed on the next tick. You will not normally call this; it is here so an operator can see what is waiting, and because the collection documents every RPC on the internal surface.

Delivers one message from the transactional outbox: claims the row `for update`, sends it on core-api's configured SMTP channel, and records the outcome, in one transaction on the agent pool. **Served as of ENT-256 (part three).** Required scope: `internal:ingest`.

**This is the activity behind every `deliver-message/{id}` workflow**, and the contract is written for being retried. A message already sent, abandoned by the reclaim, or gone answers `outcome: OUTCOME_ALREADY_SETTLED` and succeeds, so a retry after a timeout never sends twice. A refused send answers `unavailable` after the attempt and the mail server's reply have been written to the row; the worker's retry policy (ten seconds, doubling, capped at ten minutes, no attempt limit) decides when to try again. No configured channel answers `failed_precondition` naming `KINDLAST_SMTP_ADDR`, and is retried too, because the row is exactly as deliverable once the setting exists.

`messageId` comes from List undelivered. A value that is not a uuid is `invalid_argument` and the worker does not retry it. Calling this by hand delivers a real message to the real recipient, so on a laptop stack check Mailpit at http://localhost:8025 afterwards rather than an inbox.

Clears the personal data out of messages that no longer need it (ENT-242, migration 00030): redacts the recipient's address and the rendered body from delivered messages after seven days, and gives up on undelivered messages whose invitation can no longer be accepted, marking them `failed`. **Served as of ENT-256 (part three).** Required scope: `internal:ingest`.

It is the activity behind the `reclaim-transactional-outbox` Temporal Schedule, hourly at forty past. The window (seven days, `postgres.InvitationLifetime`) is a decision and lives in core-api; the rule that a message which can still be delivered is never touched is an invariant and lives in the database's definer function, where no caller of this RPC can reach past it. Idempotent: a second pass in the same hour reports zero for both counts.

The response carries `redacted`, `abandoned` and `ranAt`.

Works out who a finding notification goes to, and when, as of now. **Served as of ENT-256 (part three, second half).** Required scope: `internal:ingest`. Read only and side-effect free: for each candidate recipient (a member of the organisation with a deliverable address, via the `notification_recipients` definer function) one of three decisions, decided in Go from the raw preference fields: `DECISION_SEND`, they want it and nothing is in the way; `DECISION_HOLD` with `holdUntil`, they want it and are inside their quiet hours, so the moment their window ends in their own zone; `DECISION_SKIP` with `reason`, the finding is below their severity floor.

This is the first verb of the `deliver-notification/{id}` workflow, and it is asked again after every hold rather than once, because a hold can be nine hours and preferences change. A row that is no longer pending answers `settled: true`. The answer carries user ids, decisions and times, never an address, because it lands in a workflow history.

`notificationId` comes from List undelivered's `notificationIds`.

Sends one finding notification to the named recipients, now. **Served as of ENT-256 (part three, second half).** Required scope: `internal:ingest`. One transaction on the agent pool, row locked `for update`, one unsubscribe token and (for a verified address) one approve link minted per person, one email per person, exactly as the in-process loop did. The row is **not** marked sent here: the workflow may still be holding other recipients, and `sent` is one fact about the whole notification, recorded by Settle notification.

A refused send is recorded on the row (attempts, the server's answer) and answers `unavailable` for the retry policy. No mail channel answers `failed_precondition` naming `KINDLAST_SMTP_ADDR`; no console address answers the same naming `KINDLAST_APP_BASE_URL`, because every notification carries a link into `/o/{slug}/`. Somebody named in `userIds` who is no longer a recipient is left out rather than failing the call. Calling this by hand sends real mail; on a laptop stack read it in Mailpit at http://localhost:8025.

Marks a finding notification sent or skipped, once the workflow has nobody left to send to. **Served as of ENT-256 (part three, second half).** Required scope: `internal:ingest`. Idempotent: a row already settled answers `settled: false` and changes nothing.

`OUTCOME_SENT` when at least one email left; `OUTCOME_SKIPPED` when nobody wanted it, in which case `reason` is required and stored on the row, so an operator asking "why did nothing go out" gets an answer. `skipped` rather than `sent` is not cosmetic: `sent` means an email left the building, and a delivery no message supports would be a claim in the database that is not true.

Posture, open counts by severity, and when the agents last ran. Required scope: `dashboard:read`, kept separate from `findings:read` so a viewer can be shown the summary without being entitled to every finding behind it. **Implemented as of ENT-203**, and reachable by a signed-in human as of ENT-221; see List findings for why this collection's own token is not.

**`posture` has four values, and the fourth is the point:** `green`, `amber`, `red`, `not_assessed`. Before the Watcher has ever run there are no findings, and a posture derived by counting them reports green — telling a customer they are on track when the product has not looked (ENT-161). `not_assessed` is the only honest answer at that point.

`pipeline` is what the agent rail (ENT-222) renders. `watcherLastRunAt` is absent when the Watcher has never run for this organisation, read from `compliance_profiles.watcher_last_run_at`. `profileExists` separates "the agents have not run" from "there is nothing for them to run against", which are different problems with different fixes.

**Nothing currently runs the sweeps**, and that is deliberate rather than broken: 00001 dropped the three pg_cron jobs and the schedules move to Temporal at build-order step 8. So even a correct dashboard shows `not_assessed` until something invokes `run_watcher()` explicitly.

The caller's own notification settings for the organisation the header names. **Implemented as of ENT-209.** Required scope: `notifications:read`.

**There is no user id in the request, and there will not be one.** `notification_preferences` is keyed `(org_id, user_id)` and its policies are the only ones in the schema that pin `user_id` to `app.current_user_id`, so the row is the caller's by policy rather than by argument. A parameter would invite a client to pass somebody else's and make the handler the thing that refuses, when the policy already does.

Preferences are **personal within an organisation**. Somebody in two organisations holds two sets and can want a weekly briefing from one and silence from the other.

**Never answers not-found.** Somebody who has never opened the settings page has no row and is nonetheless subscribed, because the product default is that a member is told: the opposite default means a critical finding sits unread until each person individually opts in. So this returns defaults (`medium` and above, briefing on, deadline alerts on, `Europe/Tallinn`) rather than an error, and "I have not changed anything" stays distinguishable from a fault.

Replace the caller's own settings. **Implemented as of ENT-209.** Required scope: `notifications:write`, which `notifications:read` does not satisfy: scope matching is exact, never by prefix.

**A whole-object write, not a patch.** The settings surface renders every field at once, and a partial update would mean deciding what an absent field means, where "unset" and "set to false" are different intentions a proto3 scalar cannot tell apart. The REST alias is `PUT /api/v1/notification-preferences` for the same reason, unlike the records surface which is `PATCH`: here the body genuinely is the resource, with no server-owned columns to preserve.

`minSeverityForEmail` is a **floor**, one of `low`, `medium`, `high`, `critical`. Not a switch, because "tell me everything" trains people to ignore the mail and "tell me nothing" is how a critical finding goes unread.

`email` empty means "use the address I sign in with". It is a separate field because a compliance contact is often a shared mailbox nobody signs in as.

Quiet hours are local `HH:MM` and **may wrap midnight**: `22:00` to `07:00` means what it looks like. Both empty means no quiet window; one alone is refused, because "quiet from 22:00" with no end reads to a person as overnight and would behave as no quiet hours at all.

Answers `invalid_argument` for an unknown severity, an IANA timezone that will not load, a time that is not `HH:MM`, or half a quiet window. The timezone is checked here rather than at send time, because an unloadable zone at send time is a notification that fails hours later for a reason nobody connects to a settings page.

The response is re-read from the database rather than echoed, so it describes what is stored.

Which channels this deployment can actually deliver on (§18.3). **Implemented as of ENT-209.** Required scope: `notifications:read`.

Exists so a console never renders a channel it cannot deliver on. Telegram, Slack and WhatsApp are in the design and are not built, and they are **absent from this response rather than listed as unavailable**: a settings page offering a switch that silently does nothing is indistinguishable from a broken integration, and generates support instead of value.

`email` is present always and `available` is false on a deployment with no `KINDLAST_SMTP_ADDR`, carrying a plain-language `unavailableReason` for the console to show. Read from configuration rather than probed, because a mail server that happens to be down is not the same as a deployment that was never told where to submit mail, and only the second is worth telling a person about.

Deployment-wide rather than tenant-scoped: the answer is the same for every organisation in an installation. The organisation header is still sent because the chain requires it.

Spend an unsubscribe token. **Implemented as of ENT-209.**

**The only endpoint in this collection with no Authorization header and no organisation header, and that is the whole point.** The person clicking an unsubscribe link is reading an email, may never have signed in, and requiring them to authenticate in order to stop mail they did not ask for is how a product earns a spam complaint instead of an unsubscribe. So the token is the only identity claim, which is why it is stored hashed, expires after 30 days, and is spent once.

It is therefore **not on the Connect surface**: every method there runs behind authentication, a scope check and tenancy, and this caller has none of them. It is a plain route on core-api's mux beside `/healthz`.

**POST rather than GET, deliberately.** Corporate mail gateways and link scanners follow every URL in a message before a human sees it, so under a GET the act of delivering the email would unsubscribe the recipient. `web` renders a confirmation page at `/unsubscribe/{token}` and posts here.

**404 for every unusable token**, whether expired, already redeemed, of the wrong kind, or never real. Distinguishing them would make this an oracle for which tokens exist, to a caller who has proved nothing. 404 rather than 401 for the same reason: 401 invites a client to authenticate and there is nothing to authenticate as.

On success it returns the organisation the token named, and turns off the weekly briefing and deadline alerts and raises the email floor to `critical` for that person in that organisation alone.

To try it on the local stack: trigger a finding, read the message in Mailpit at `http://localhost:8025`, and copy the token out of the unsubscribe link.

item.name: Approve a finding from an email link (no session)

request.description:
Spend §8's one-tap approve link. **Implemented as of ENT-249.**

The second endpoint with no Authorization header and no organisation header, and the only one that writes to a customer's compliance record without a session. The person clicking is reading an email and may never have signed in, so the delegation is the whole identity claim: stored hashed, expiring within the hour, spent once, and bound to the one finding named beside it.

**This is NOT a widened `capability_tokens.kind`.** ENT-209 constrained that column to `unsubscribe` alone and this consumer leaves it there. `redeem_capability_token` PERFORMS the act inside redemption, so widening it would put a second implementation of approval in plpgsql beside the one in Go. A delegation performs nothing: it answers "who is this", and the ordinary act path does the rest. That is what makes an approval from an email indistinguishable in the database from the same person's approval at the keyboard, except in the channel named beside it.

**POST rather than GET, and here it matters more than anywhere else in this collection.** Corporate mail gateways, link previewers and archiving proxies fetch every URL in a message before a human sees it. Under a GET the act of DELIVERING a finding notification would approve the finding, with an audit row naming somebody who never opened the message: findings approving themselves in transit. The route is registered POST-only, so every other method answers 405 without reaching anything that can approve. `web` renders an interstitial at `{{web_base_url}}/approve/{findingId}/{token}` and posts here.

**BOTH HALVES ARE REQUIRED, AND THAT IS DEFENCE IN DEPTH RATHER THAN VALIDATION.** `resolve_act_delegation` matches the presented finding against the delegation's binding with `is not distinct from`. A token recovered on its own, from a mail relay's log or a truncated URL, approves nothing. The symmetry also means an approve link CANNOT be presented in the `Kindlast-Delegation` header: that path resolves unbound delegations only, so a credential minted to approve one finding is not a session for everything that person can do.

**404 for every unusable link**, whether expired, revoked, already redeemed, minted for a different finding, minted for somebody since removed from the organisation, or never real. Missing halves answer the same 404 rather than a helpful 400, because a 400 would tell a caller which request shape is worth making.

On success it returns `{ "orgSlug", "findingId", "applied" }`. The slug is where the interstitial sends the person next, and it comes from the organisation the delegation named rather than from anything the request carried: §8's named failure is a consultant with three clients acting against the wrong company from a stale link. `applied: false` means the finding was already approved, which is a second click or a colleague getting there first rather than an error.

**The approval records `approval_reviewed = false`.** A doorbell says that something happened and not what it says, so somebody deciding from their mailbox has not read the finding. The message says so before the click and the trail says so afterwards.

**There is no mint endpoint, for this or for any delegation.** These are minted by the doorbell dispatcher through `mint_finding_approval_delegation`, which takes an outbox row the dispatcher has already claimed rather than an organisation and a finding, so it cannot pair a person with a finding it was not sent to deliver. A delegation is never minted for an address the IdP did not say was verified, including a `notification_preferences` override address, which nobody has proved anything about.

To try it on the local stack: trigger a finding, read the message in Mailpit at `http://localhost:8025`, and copy the finding id and token out of the approve link. Note that the recipient must have signed in at least once since migration 00027, because `user_identities.email_verified` is not backfilled and an unverified address gets the doorbell without a link.

The Article 30 record of processing activities. Required scope: `records:read`.

**Served as of ENT-200.** Approving a `create_ropa` finding already writes a row here, and the console renders this register at /o/{slug}/records.

Pagination is keyset over `(org_id, created_at desc)`, not offset, for the reason List findings gives. `pageToken` is opaque: do not parse or construct one. Treat a non-empty `nextPageToken` as the only signal that more exist.

**Ordered by creation, not by `updated_at`**, which is a deliberate change from the legacy console. Ordering a paginated list by a column that changes under it lets a row edited between two page requests be skipped or returned twice. "What did I touch last" is a sort a client can offer within a page.

**`completeness` is computed server-side**, one of `complete`, `incomplete`, `review_needed`. `review_needed` means the Executor pre-filled the entry and no human has edited it since, which is a different state from incomplete and wants a different prompt. `complete` additionally requires the row to have been updated after it was created, which is what stops a stub from ever reading as complete without a human having looked.

**`manualQuota`** carries the Free-tier cap on manually-created activities (ENT-84). `limit: 0` means unlimited, which is what a paid plan and a billing-disabled self-hosted deployment both report — check for zero rather than rendering "3 of 0 used". Executor-created rows never count against it: a record created from an approved finding is part of the compliance record and is not withheld behind a plan.

One entry in the Article 30 record. Required scope: `records:read`. **Served as of ENT-200.**

**The empty fields are the point, not a gap.** `approve_finding` creates the row from a finding that knows the activity exists and not what is in it, so `purpose`, `legalBasis` and `retentionPeriod` come back empty on an Executor-created stub. Article 30 is a record of fact, and a plausible guess in `legalBasis` is the single worst thing this product could write.

`sourceFindingId` is set when the Executor created this and empty when a human did. "Why is this here" is the first question an auditor asks of a compliance record.

The AI Act system register. Required scope: `records:read`. **Served as of ENT-200.** Approving an `ai-act-annex-iii-high-risk-systems` or `ai-act-art-26-deployer-obligations` finding already writes a row here (00009).

**`riskClassification` defaults to `unclassified`, deliberately not `minimal`.** Article 6 classification is a judgement with consequences, and a register defaulting to the lowest tier tells a customer they are fine about a system nobody has assessed. Same reasoning as `not_assessed` on the dashboard posture, applied to a record instead of a summary. Values: `unacceptable`, `high`, `limited`, `minimal`, `unclassified`.

`documentationStatus` is `missing`, `in_progress` or `complete`: how far the Article 11 technical documentation has got.

`lastReviewedAt` absent means never reviewed, which for a register driving high-risk obligations is worth showing rather than hiding behind a created date.

**Measured, and worth knowing before you profile this:** `ai_systems` carried only an `(org_id)` index from 00002 while its two sibling registers had the composite. Migration 00011 adds `(org_id, created_at desc)` and drops the redundant single-column index, because a keyset page over an unsupported ordering sorts the whole tenant's rows on every request.

One system in the AI Act register. Required scope: `records:read`. **Served as of ENT-200.**

`vendor` empty means built in house, which is a meaningful empty rather than a missing one: the AI Act's provider and deployer duties differ, and an organisation that built the system is generally both.

Data-subject access requests and the statutory clock on each. Required scope: `records:read`. **Served as of ENT-200.**

**Ordered by `responseDueAt` ascending, soonest first**, not by creation, because the only question anyone asks of a DSAR log is which one runs out next. That means a `pageToken` from this list is **not** interchangeable with the ones from the other two registers. Migration 00011 adds the `(org_id, response_due_at)` index this needs; the pre-existing `dsars_due_idx` looks like the right index and is not, because it does not lead with `org_id` and is partial on the two unfinished statuses.

**Nothing in this register arrives from an approval, unlike the other two.** 00009 classified three obligations and deliberately mapped none to `create_dsar`, and 00010 asserts that: a data-subject request arrives from a person, so an obligation that manufactured one would be inventing the requester. Every row here was logged by a human, and `sourceFindingId` is therefore always empty today. It is carried rather than omitted so that going from always-empty to sometimes-set is not a contract change.

**`urgency` is computed server-side**, one of `overdue`, `due_soon`, `on_track`, `answered`, with `due_soon` meaning ten days or fewer remaining. That window is a regulatory escalation threshold, and a client re-deriving it from `responseDueAt` would be a second implementation of a deadline that would eventually disagree with this one. `daysUntilDue` is carried alongside it because "4 days left" and "11 days overdue" are the words a handler acts on.

`status` filters to `open`, `in_progress`, `responded` or `closed`. Omit it for every status: a closed request is still part of the record an auditor asks to see.

**`trailEntryCount` is how much evidence stands behind each request (ENT-226).** It is on the list and not only on the read because it is the number that makes `respondedAt` checkable at a glance: a request marked responded with a zero here is an assertion with nothing under it. Connect's JSON drops zero values, so an absent field means zero. Nothing refuses `MarkDsarResponded` on a zero, deliberately: a customer who assembled the response elsewhere has still met the deadline, and a rule that Article 12(3) requires a Kindlast trail would be an obligation the law does not contain.

One data-subject request. Required scope: `records:read`. **Served as of ENT-200.**

**`receivedAt` is not the row's creation timestamp and the two routinely differ (ENT-224).** A request that arrived by post on the 1st and was logged on the 8th is due one month from the 1st. Article 12(3) runs from receipt, so a clock started at data entry silently grants the organisation the days it took them to notice, which is exactly backwards. `00010_dsar_clock_from_receipt.sql` made the executor path refuse a missing, non-timestamp or future `received_at` rather than defaulting to `now()`.

`responseDueAt` is stored rather than computed on read, so an extension is recorded as a fact about this request instead of being re-derived from a rule that may since have changed. The Article 12(3) two-month extension for complex requests is **not yet modelled**; 00010 left it open as a schema question.

`requestType` is free text rather than an enum on purpose: Article 15-22 requests arrive worded by the person making them, and forcing them into a closed list at intake loses what was actually asked for.

`trailEntryCount` carries how many trail entries stand behind this request (ENT-226). The entries themselves come from **List DSAR trail**: they are free text about a named data subject and a register response has no business carrying all of it.

Adds an Article 30 entry the Executor has not seen. Required scope: `records:ropa:write`, which is deliberately not `records:read`. **Served as of ENT-200.**

**Capped on the free plan, and over the cap answers `resource_exhausted`, not `permission_denied`.** The caller is entitled to do this and has run out of allowance, which is a distinction with a button under it: one has an upgrade, the other sends somebody to an owner who cannot help. The cap counts only manually created rows, because a record created from an approved finding is part of the compliance record and is never withheld behind a plan.

**`failed_precondition` here means the organisation has no compliance profile**, so there is nothing for a record to hang off. Finish onboarding first.

There is no actor field and there will not be one. `The store reads the acting human from the session GUC, enforces the cap, and writes the audit row in the same transaction as the insert. A handler writing the table directly would have to reimplement all three.

Replaces an entry's fields. Required scope: `records:ropa:write`. **Served as of ENT-200.**

**A full replacement, not a patch, and the field mask that would make it a patch is deliberately absent.** Article 30 is a record of fact whose gaps are meaningful: clearing a legal basis is a real edit somebody makes when they realise the one recorded was wrong, and a partial update in which an omitted field means "leave it alone" gives a client no way to express that. Send every field you want the record to have.

An unknown id and one belonging to another organisation both answer `not_found`, because the database function's lookup is org-scoped and cannot tell them apart either.

Registers a system nobody has approved a finding about. Required scope: `records:ai-systems:write`. **Served as of ENT-200.**

Useful mostly for shadow AI: the system somebody adopted without telling anyone is exactly the one no finding will ever raise.

**`reviewed` is required when `riskClassification` is `high`**, and the body above will answer `failed_precondition` if you set it to false. See Update AI system for why.

An empty `riskClassification` means `unclassified`, which is the honest default and deliberately not `minimal`: a register that defaulted to the lowest tier would tell a customer they are fine about a system nobody has assessed.

Replaces a system's fields. Required scope: `records:ai-systems:write`. **Served as of ENT-200.**

**ANY change to `riskClassification` is refused unless `reviewed` is true**, and the refusal is `failed_precondition` rather than `permission_denied`: the caller may do this and must confirm first, so a console shows a confirm step rather than an upgrade prompt or an owner's name.

The reason is that an Article 6 classification is the determination the whole high-risk obligation stack hangs off. Moving a system out of `high` in a form somebody was tabbing through would quietly retire Articles 9 to 17 for it, and the record would show a change with nobody's deliberate decision behind it. `reviewed` says a human meant it, and the audit row records that they did.

**An edit that leaves the classification alone needs no confirmation**, which is what keeps the gate from being a nuisance on every save. **The gate lives in Go as of ENT-225**, and this sentence used to say the opposite. It read: "the gate lives in `update_ai_system`, not in the handler: a check in Go would be a second implementation, and the copy furthest from the data is the one that drifts." That was a reasonable argument and it lost. A classification change requiring a reviewed approval is a decision, not an invariant, and 00016 dropped the function. There is exactly one implementation either way; what changed is which language it is in and whether it can be table-tested without a database.

Records a request that arrived. Required scope: `records:dsar:write`. **Served as of ENT-200.**

**This is the only way a DSAR enters the register.** Nothing creates one from an approval: 00009 classified three obligations and mapped none to `create_dsar`, because a request comes from a person and an obligation that manufactured one would be inventing the requester.

**`receivedAt` decides the deadline, and omitting it means today (ENT-224).** Before migration 00012 there was no such field: `log_dsar` stamped `now()`, so a request that came by post on the 1st and was logged on the 8th was recorded as due a month from the 8th. Article 12(3) runs from receipt, so a clock started at data entry silently grants the organisation the days it took them to notice, and the slower they are the longer they appear to have.

A **future date is refused** with `invalid_argument` rather than clamped: a request cannot have arrived tomorrow, and the likeliest cause is a typo that would extend a statutory deadline nobody chose to extend. `invalid_argument` rather than `failed_precondition` because the fix is a different value, not a condition to satisfy and retry.

The response carries the computed `responseDueAt`, which is the field the person who logged it actually needs to know.

`subjectName` is optional: a request can arrive pseudonymously, through a form or an inbox, before anyone has identified the person behind it. `handler` is optional and free text, because it is often a role or an external DPO rather than a member of the workspace.

Records that a response went out, which stops the statutory clock. Required scope: `records:dsar:write`. **Served as of ENT-200.**

**`reviewed` must be true**, for the same class of reason Update AI system needs it: this is the assertion that the organisation met an Article 12(3) deadline, and it is the single most consequential row in this register to get wrong. A regulator reading the log later is reading this field. Without it, `failed_precondition`.

**Idempotent.** Marking an already-answered request returns `applied: false` and writes nothing, rather than overwriting the date a response actually went out with the date somebody clicked the button twice. The status is read BEFORE the call rather than after, which matters: reading it afterwards reports `applied` on every repeat, and that is a bug the findings act path shipped with and had to fix.

**This is no longer the only evidence a deadline was met (ENT-226).** `respondedAt` on its own is an assertion: it says a response went out and cannot show what was searched, what was found or what was returned. **Add DSAR trail entry** is what stands behind it, and `trailEntryCount` on the request says how much. This call still does not require one, and that is deliberate rather than unfinished: a customer who assembled the response outside Kindlast has still met the deadline.

**Worth knowing if you script against this:** each request gets its own transaction, so a refusal costs nothing, but two writes in one request will see the second fail with `25P02` for a reason unrelated to it if the first was refused.

The trail a response to this request was assembled from. Required scope: `records:read`. **Served as of ENT-226.**

**What it is for.** `respondedAt` says a response went out and nothing more. A regulator reading the register cannot see what was searched, what was found, or what was returned, which for a product whose claim is that a human can check a claim was the weakest row in it. These entries are that record: they are the customer's evidence rather than an internal trace, and they are readable and exportable.

**Ordered oldest first, which is the opposite of every other list on this service.** The registers answer "what is outstanding" and lead with the most pressing row; a trail answers "what did you do", and that reads forward. So a `pageToken` from this list is not interchangeable with any other here.

**Ordered by `occurredAt`, not by `recordedAt`.** Both are on every entry and they are different facts: a handler who searched the CRM on Tuesday and wrote it up on Friday did one thing, and a trail that only knew Friday could not show the search happened inside the statutory month. The gap between them is itself informative, so both are carried.

`action` is one of `searched`, `found`, `none_found`, `disclosed`, `withheld`. `none_found` is not the same as the absence of an entry: "we looked in the CRM and there was nothing" and "nobody has looked in the CRM" are different facts.

Answers `not_found` for a request in another organisation, exactly as **Get DSAR** does, because RLS makes a request that does not exist and one that is not yours the same query result.

Appends one step to a request's trail. Required scope: `records:dsar:write`. **Served as of ENT-226.**

**Append only, and there is no update or delete call to go with it.** Not an unfinished surface: the entry is evidence about how a response to a statutory request was built, and evidence a producer can revise afterwards is worth less than evidence it cannot. `dsar_trail_entries` refuses an UPDATE with a trigger that binds even `kindlast_migrator`, and `kindlast_app` holds no DELETE grant, so an RPC for either could not be served whatever the contract said. **A correction is another entry.**

**`source` is free text and deliberately not an enum.** The stores are the customer's own estate, so a closed list here would be Kindlast enumerating somebody else's systems, the same mistake `requestType` avoids. Where a request reaches data Kindlast itself holds, the three stores in `docs/personal-data-runbook.md` are the names to use. Blank or whitespace-only is `invalid_argument`.

**`action` must be one of `searched`, `found`, `none_found`, `disclosed`, `withheld`**, and anything else is `invalid_argument` naming the set. `withheld` is a first-class outcome because Article 15(4) and the Member State exemptions are real: a response that leaves something out for a stated reason is lawful, and one that leaves something out silently is evidence of nothing. The reason goes in `detail`.

**`occurredAt` is when the search happened; omit it for now.** A future value is refused with `invalid_argument` rather than clamped, for the same reason a future `receivedAt` is on **Log DSAR**: the point of the field is when the search actually happened, and a value the server quietly rewrote is a worse record than a refusal you can fix. `recordedAt` is stamped by the database and is never something you send.
