**`agentRunId` is provenance and is validated against what you can see.** It is refused with `invalid_argument` unless it names a run in your own organisation, so an entry can never be attributed to another tenant's run: the foreign key alone would allow that, because referential checks do not run under row security. `createdBy` is taken from the verified token and never from the body, so an entry always says which human filed it whatever it claims about a run. **Empty from every caller that exists today**; it is in the contract because the integrations gateway (§26.4) writes through this call, and provenance added afterwards is provenance nobody recorded.

**No `reviewed` gate, unlike Mark DSAR responded.** Recording that you searched the CRM is not an assertion a regulator reads as compliance; it is the working note that makes the assertion checkable, and a confirm step on every note would mean fewer notes.

An access to a data subject's data in service of a DSAR is still an access, so every call here writes an `audit_log` row with `actionType` `add_dsar_trail_entry` in the same transaction as the entry.

What this organisation is on, and what this deployment can offer it. Required scope: `billing:read`. **Served as of ENT-210.**

**Read only, and BillingService has no write RPC at all.** A plan changes because a payment provider's signed webhook said so. An endpoint that could change one from a session would be a way to grant yourself a paid entitlement with a request, so it does not exist rather than existing behind a check.

**Owner-only, refused with `permission_denied` for a member.** The scope says what a token may attempt and the role says who inside the organisation may; a member holds `billing:read` like everybody else, so the handler checks the role as well. The console renders 404 rather than the refusal, because "you are not allowed" is itself information about the organisation.

**`plan` and `status` are different questions and both are returned.** `plan` is the entitlement in force, so a `pro` subscription that is `past_due` or `canceled` reports `plan: "free"` here. A client that rendered only `plan` would tell a paying customer whose card was declined that they had downgraded themselves, which is why `status` is carried separately.

**`billingConfigured` is read from configuration, not inferred from the absence of a subscription row.** A hosted customer between provisioning and their first row looks identical to a self-hoster, and would otherwise be shown a page saying the product cannot be bought. `gatingEnabled` is separate again, because an operator may wire a provider before turning gating on, and then nothing is withheld and nothing should be advertised as withheld.

An organisation that has never bought anything has no subscription row and reports `plan: "free"` with an empty `status`.

Applies a payment provider's subscription event. **Implemented as of ENT-210.**

**Unauthenticated, and it changes what a customer is entitled to.** No session, no token, no caller identity: anybody on the internet can POST here. The only thing separating a real event from an invented one is the HMAC in `Stripe-Signature`, which is why it is verified **before the body is parsed** and before anything is read out of it. A handler that unmarshals first has already let the caller choose what its parser sees.

Not on the Connect surface for the same reason as Unsubscribe: every method there runs behind authentication, a scope check and tenancy, and this caller has none of them. It is a plain route on core-api's mux, and the edge routes exactly this one path to core-api rather than the whole `/api/v1/*` prefix.

**Signing a request by hand**, which you must do because Postman cannot compute it for you:

```
t=$(date +%s)
body='{"id":"evt_local_001",...}'   # byte for byte what you send
printf '%s.%s' "$t" "$body" \
  | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$KINDLAST_BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET" -hex
```

Then send `Stripe-Signature: t=<t>,v1=<hex>`. The signed payload is `timestamp + "." + raw body`, so any reformatting of the JSON invalidates it. The header may carry several `v1=` values and any one matching is accepted, which is what makes a secret rotation not an outage.

**The timestamp is checked in both directions**, five minutes either side. A signature would otherwise be valid forever, and a timestamp far in the future is as much a forgery signal as one far in the past.

**Every refusal is a bare 4xx with no body.** No signature, a bad signature and an expired one are indistinguishable to the caller on purpose: an endpoint that explains why it refused is one an attacker can use to search for a working forgery.

**Replays return 200 and change nothing.** The event id is claimed in the same transaction as the subscription write, so a retried delivery hits the primary key and the whole transaction rolls back. Providers retry on any non-2xx and on timeouts, so a 4xx here would be retried forever and a 500 would be retried on something already applied.

**An unknown customer is also 200 and also records nothing**, deliberately: a customer this deployment has not seen may be one whose checkout has not landed yet, and burning the event id would make the provider's retry a permanent no-op.

**Only three event types do anything**: `customer.subscription.created`, `.updated` and `.deleted`. An allow-list rather than a switch with a default, so a provider adding a type cannot silently start moving plans. Everything else is acknowledged and ignored.

The plan comes from the price's **`lookup_key`**, not its id: a price id is generated per environment and would make this deployment-specific. Anything other than `pro` reads as `free`, and any status this code does not recognise reads as `canceled`, because an unknown must never grant.

The request runs on its own Postgres role, `kindlast_billing`, which holds grants on two tables and nothing else. It resolves the customer to an organisation through its one unscoped select, sets `app.current_org_id` to what it resolved, and only then writes: a crafted payload cannot turn one event into an upgrade for a different tenant, because the write matches zero rows rather than the wrong ones.

To try it locally, set `KINDLAST_BILLING_ENABLED=true` and a `KINDLAST_BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET` in the compose environment, and give an organisation a `provider_customer_id` to resolve against.

What this deployment checks organisations against. Required scope: `corpus:read`. **Served as of ENT-207.**

**The only service in `core.v1` whose data is not tenant data.** The corpus has no `org_id`: it is the same regulation for every customer, and ENT-207 says in terms not to give it one to make it look like the rest of the schema. ENT-192's ten public-read policies carry that, so every member of every organisation reads the same rows.

The organisation header is still required. That keeps one shape for every request on this surface, and it means a caller has to be a member of something: the law is public, but this deployment's copy of it is not a public API.

**Read only, and there is no write RPC anywhere in `core.v1` for this.** Writing the corpus is `IngestService` on `/internal/v1`, behind `internal:ingest`, on the `kindlast_ingest` Postgres role which holds grants on the ten regulatory tables and cannot read a finding. That separation is the product's central claim: a customer trusts a finding because they can check it against the law, which only means something if the thing serving the claim cannot edit the law.

**No role gate.** Every member sees this, viewers included.

**Unpaged**, deliberately: there are fifteen obligations, they change when a regulation changes rather than when a customer does something, and a keyset cursor would be machinery for a page that fits on a screen. Ordered worst-first by severity rather than alphabetically, because `high` sorts after `low` and `medium` and that is the wrong way round.

**`citation` is the SAME message FindingsService returns**, imported rather than redeclared. Render `citation.label` and link `citation.url`; do not rebuild either from the parts. Two implementations of "what is this citation called" diverge the first time a regulation needs a special case.

**A label reading like `32016R0679 Art. 30` instead of `GDPR Art. 30` means something specific**: `analyst_citation_label` fell through to its raw-CELEX fallback because no document with that CELEX is in the corpus. That was the state of every obligation in this product before ENT-207 filled the tables, and it is what an unloaded deployment looks like.

`severity` here is the law's view of the duty, the same for every customer. It says nothing about whether any organisation is failing it; that is the findings feed.

One obligation, with the regulatory text behind it. Required scope: `corpus:read`. **Served as of ENT-207.**

Keyed by **slug**, not by id, and that is deliberate. A slug is stable across rewordings of the obligation text, so `gdpr-art-30-ropa` is a key somebody can put in a document; the row's uuid is generated per deployment and would differ between two installations reading the same law.

**404 for an unknown slug, plainly.** None of the care the tenant surfaces take about telling "does not exist" from "not yours" applies: the corpus is the same for everybody, so an unknown slug is simply unknown and saying so leaks nothing.

`citedSummary`, `citedHeading` and `citedParagraphSummary` are the text the citation points at. **They are OUR summaries, not the Official Journal wording.** The corpus stores no verbatim text: every article, recital and annex row carries a curated 1-2000 character summary, and the authoritative wording lives at `citation.url`. A client showing this must say so, because a reader deciding whether to act on a finding needs to know they are reading a paraphrase.

**An empty `citedSummary` is a real condition rather than a blank.** Ingest refuses to store an obligation whose citation resolves to nothing, so reaching it here means either the corpus was written some other way or a regulation was loaded without the one this cites.

Which regulations this deployment holds, and how much of each. Required scope: `corpus:read`. **Served as of ENT-207.**

Exists so a console can say "the GDPR, 99 articles, as at 4 May 2016" rather than leaving a customer to wonder whether the corpus is current. **A compliance product that cannot say which version of the law it is working from is asking for trust it has not earned**, and the counts plus `versionDate` plus the CELEX number are a claim a reader can check in one click through `officialUrl`.

**An empty list is the most important response this returns.** It means no regulation has been ingested, which makes every citation on every finding fall back to a raw CELEX number, and it is a condition an operator can fix rather than a bug. A console should say so rather than render an empty panel.

After loading `data/corpus/` this reports the GDPR (99 articles, 173 recitals) and the EU AI Act (113 articles, 180 recitals, 1 annex).

What Kindlast currently believes about the organisation. Required scope: `memory:read`. **Served as of ENT-228.**

This is the surface that makes the memory the customer's. §26.5 puts memory in Postgres under RLS rather than in an agent framework's store precisely so a customer can see it, correct it, export it and have it erased, and a schema alone does not deliver that. **A GDPR product whose own memory of a customer sits outside that customer's reach cannot answer a request about it.**

**Open values only.** Each fact is one row believed over one interval, and this returns the interval that has not been closed. History is `GetFactHistory` and is a different question; returning both here would make the common read carry every superseded value the organisation has ever had.

**Unpaged**, deliberately: the profile is a few dozen facts by construction, and somebody asking what a product knows about them wants the answer rather than a window onto it.

`source` is shown against each value rather than against the profile as a whole, because a profile where one field came from a connected tool and another from a guess in a form is the normal case. `evidenceId` is empty for a fact a human simply stated, which is most of onboarding.

**No role gate.** Every member sees this, viewers included: a person who can be told a finding should be able to see the profile that finding was reasoned from.

Every value one fact has ever had, newest first. Required scope: `memory:read`. **Served as of ENT-228.**

**The read that makes correction meaningful.** Without it, correcting a fact is indistinguishable from our having always thought the new thing, and what somebody checking an old finding is asking is exactly what we believed at the time.

Each entry carries `validFrom` and `validTo`. An empty `validTo` is the open value. **The intervals meet exactly**: a value's `validTo` is the successor's `validFrom`, to the microsecond, because a gap however small is an instant where an as-of query finds no value and reports that we believed nothing.

That is not free and it cost an afternoon. Postgres `now()` is the TRANSACTION timestamp and is identical for every statement in a transaction, so closing with `now()` and opening with `now()` produced two rows with the same `validFrom`, a zero-length interval, and a history whose order was undefined because the column it sorts by tied. The store takes one `clock_timestamp()` and uses it for both statements. Anything writing these rows directly must do the same.

**Keyed by the fact key rather than by a row id.** A key is stable and meaningful; the id of the currently open row changes every time the fact is corrected, which is precisely when somebody wants to look at its history.

**Each entry carries `note`, the reason the value was recorded.** It is whatever the person wrote when they corrected the fact, and it is the only part of the record that says why a value changed rather than what it changed to. Empty for most entries: onboarding answers carry none, and the note is optional on a correction. It was accepted by CorrectFact and stored from the beginning but returned by nothing until ProfileFact gained the field, so a client written against an older response will simply not see it.

Correct a fact, as a typed patch. Required scope: `memory:write`. **Served as of ENT-228.**

**Never an update in place.** It closes the current value and records a new one, in one transaction. `kindlast_app` holds `update (valid_to)` and NOT `update (value)`, so an in-place rewrite is refused by the database rather than avoided by convention. "Updated only by typed patches, never free-text rewrite" is a promise until it is a privilege, and it is a privilege you can read out of `information_schema.column_privileges`.

**`value` is a oneof and the arm must match the key.** `text` for `INDUSTRY`; `list` for `EU_JURISDICTIONS`, `DATA_CATEGORIES`, `DATA_SUBJECTS`, `AI_SYSTEMS`, `TRANSFER_DESTINATIONS`, `LAWFUL_BASES`; `number` for `STAFF_COUNT`; `triState` for `HAS_DPO`, `HAS_ROPA`, `TRANSFERS_OUTSIDE_EU`, `HIGH_RISK_PROCESSING`, `HIGH_RISK_AI_SYSTEM`, `LARGE_SCALE_MONITORING`. The wrong arm is `invalid_argument`, checked in Go before anything is written: the oneof stops you sending two arms at once but not the wrong one, and jsonb would store `"about fifty"` as a staff count happily.

**Four of these keys decide whether an obligation applies** (ENT-246). `HIGH_RISK_PROCESSING`, `HIGH_RISK_AI_SYSTEM`, `LARGE_SCALE_MONITORING` and `LAWFUL_BASES` are read by the Watcher: an organisation that has not answered them is NOT bound by the obligations that narrow on them, because asserting a Data Protection Impact Assessment from silence is a fabricated obligation and an expensive one. `TRI_STATE_UNSURE` counts as applying, since "we asked and they did not know" is not "they said no". `LAWFUL_BASES` takes members of Article 6(1): `consent`, `contract`, `legal_obligation`, `vital_interests`, `public_task`, `legitimate_interests`, and anything else is `invalid_argument`, because the Watcher matches those strings and a spelling nothing matches is Article 7 silently applying to nobody.

**`TRI_STATE_UNSURE` is a real answer, not a missing one.** "We do not know whether we have a record of processing activities" is a finding in itself, and collapsing it to `NO` is a different claim about the same organisation.

**`changed: false` means nothing was written.** Correcting a fact to the value it already holds is a no-op rather than a second identical row, because a history full of "changed from yes to yes" is a history nobody scrolls. The comparison is on the stored jsonb, so whitespace and key order are not changes.

**`source` is not a field you can send.** It is recorded as `human` because this RPC is reached with a user token, and a console able to label its own writes `integration` could make a guess look like an observation. `recordedBy` comes from the verified subject for the same reason: a caller naming which human corrected a fact is a caller that can attribute a change to somebody else.

**`note` is free text and is not a contradiction of any of the above.** The rule is about the VALUE. The note sits beside it and is what makes a profile change legible a year later.

**This is on `core.v1` rather than `IngestService`, and that is a deliberate departure from ENT-228's wording.** `IngestService` sits behind `internal:ingest`, issued to service principals through client credentials and never to a browser. A human correcting a fact about their own organisation holds a user token. Routing this through `IngestService` would mean either issuing internal scopes to people, undoing what ENT-207 built, or writing without the person's identity, losing `recordedBy` on the one write where "which human said so" matters most. When integrations (ENT-231) and onboarding (ENT-212) need to write facts without a human, they get their own typed patch on the platform surface.

What we observed, and where each observation came from. Required scope: `memory:read`. **Served as of ENT-228.**

Evidence and profile facts are separate on purpose. **"What do you think our lawful basis is" and "what did the tool actually return in March" are different questions**, and a schema answering both with the same rows answers the first one badly. Evidence grows forever and is never edited; the profile is small and changes.

`observedAt` is when it was true at the source; `fetchedAt` is when we learned it. Both, because they are routinely far apart and **the gap is the interesting part**: a record of processing activities last edited in March and first read by us in August is a five-month blind spot that one timestamp would hide.

**Paged**, unlike the profile, because every sweep of every connected tool adds rows. Keyset over `observedAt` descending: pass the `nextPageToken` back as `pageToken`. An offset would drift as observations arrive during paging, which on an append-only table is the normal case rather than a rare one. **A token is issued only when the page was full**, so an absent token means there is no more rather than that there might not be.

`body` is JSON as a string and is deliberately untyped, unlike a fact. An observation from a helpdesk and one from a cloud provider share nothing but their stamps, and a schema pretending otherwise would be a schema per integration.

`supersededBy` names the observation that replaced this one. Supersession is recorded rather than implied, and **dedup is an explicit operation rather than a unique constraint**: `contentHash` is indexed and not unique, because "the tool still says this in August" is a fact rather than a duplicate.

**Written by the integrations gateway as of ENT-231**, and by two doors rather than one. A live fetch a person asked for goes through `IntegrationsService.FetchNow` on `kindlast_app`, under RLS and their own membership; a machine's fetch goes through `IngestService.IngestEvidence` on `kindlast_agent`. Both write the same row with the same stamps, and neither is reachable by the other's caller, because a user token can never carry an `internal:*` scope. The gateway itself still holds no database role, exactly as this description said it would not.

`connectionId` now carries a real foreign key to `integrations`, deferrable so that erasing an organisation, which cascades into both tables, is checked once at commit rather than in an order Postgres does not promise.

Every connection this organisation has, with its tools. Required scope: `integrations:read`. **Served as of ENT-231**, and only when this deployment has a gateway: without `KINDLAST_GATEWAY_URL` and `KINDLAST_GATEWAY_TOKEN` the service is not registered at all, so you get a 404 rather than a 500. That is deliberate. A console showing an Integrations page whose every button fails looks broken; one showing no page looks unconfigured, and only the second sends an operator to the right place.

**Revoked connections stay in the list.** A customer asking what Kindlast has been able to reach is asking about the past as well as the present, and a list that quietly forgot a revoked connection could not answer them.

**No credential comes back, in any field, ever.** There is no accessor on this surface that returns one; the sealed value is read by exactly one query, at the moment a fetch is dispatched, and handed straight to the gateway.

Each tool carries `writeCapable` and `granted` separately, and the pair is the whole point: the first is what the endpoint can do, the second is what a human agreed Kindlast may do.

Asks an endpoint what tools it has, and **stores nothing**. Required scope: `integrations:write`. **Served as of ENT-231.**

**A separate call from connecting, on purpose.** Connecting in one step would mean a customer agreeing to a tool list they have not seen. This returns the list the consent screen renders; `ConnectIntegration` then records the connection along with the tools as they were shown.

**Every tool comes back with `granted: false`, without exception**, including read-only ones. A screen that arrives with boxes already ticked is a screen people click past, and the value of this one is entirely in it being read.

**`writeCapable` is the gateway's reading, and an unannotated tool reads as writing.** MCP servers may set `readOnlyHint`; many do not. The friendlier default would let a `delete_everything` tool from a server that annotates nothing through the gate marked safe, so the answer is read-only when and only when the endpoint said so.

**This is where an endpoint outside the deployment's egress allow-list is refused**, with `permission_denied` and with nothing sent to it: no DNS lookup, no TCP connection, no bytes. Discovery goes through the gateway rather than being a check core-api could make itself, so the allow-list has exactly one home and the consent screen's data comes through the same door every later fetch uses.

The credential travels in the body and is never returned. Leave it empty for an endpoint on your own network that wants none, which is a real configuration rather than a missing value.

Records the connection, its tools and the consent, in one transaction. Required scope: `integrations:write`. **Served as of ENT-231.**

**A write-capable tool is not granted by this call being made.** Every discovered tool is stored; only the ones named in `grantedTools` are callable. A tool arriving with `granted: true` already set does not become granted, which closes the obvious way to grant one without ticking it: round-tripping the discovery response.

That is three separate refusals rather than one. The column defaults to false, so a discovery insert that says nothing produces a tool nobody may call. `kindlast_app` holds `update (granted, granted_at, granted_by)` and **not** `write_capable`, so a caller cannot relabel a write tool as read-only and walk it past the gate. And the gateway refuses independently on every call, checking the endpoint's own annotation again.

**`offeredTools` is sent back rather than rediscovered**, so what is stored as consent is what the human actually saw. A second discovery between the screen and the click could return a different list, and the consent record would then describe a screen nobody looked at. A tampered `writeCapable` here changes the label a tool is stored under and not what it may do, because the gateway takes the stricter of the two readings before every call.

**A credential is refused rather than stored in plaintext when this deployment has no key.** `KINDLAST_INTEGRATION_KEY` is written `id:base64key`, AES-256; the id is recorded on every row so a key can be rotated without downtime, and the connection's own row id is bound in as additional authenticated data so a ciphertext cannot be moved between rows. A connection to an endpoint needing no credential is made whether or not a key is configured.

A grant naming a tool the endpoint did not offer is `invalid_argument` rather than being ignored: silently dropping it is how a console that has drifted out of step grants nothing while showing a tick.

Replaces which tools one connection may call. Required scope: `integrations:write`. **Served as of ENT-231.**

**A replace rather than an add-and-remove pair**, because two operations invite a client to send one of them and leave the other for later.

**Writes a new consent row rather than editing the old one.** `integration_consents` holds no update grant for anybody, so this is enforced rather than intended: widening what a product may do inside somebody's systems is exactly the change somebody will later need to reconstruct, and a table where the current state overwrote the previous one could not show it.

Refused with `failed_precondition` on a revoked connection. Revocation is terminal by design.

Stops future fetches, permanently. Required scope: `integrations:write`. **Served as of ENT-231.**

**Terminal, and reconnecting is a new connection with a new consent.** That is a deliberate refusal to make un-revoke a button: permission to reach a customer's systems should not be resurrectable by somebody who did not know why it was withdrawn. The database agrees, holding `update (status, revoked_at, revoked_by)` and a constraint pairing the status with the timestamp, so a revocation that does not say when is refused.

**Idempotent.** A second call changes nothing and returns the connection, rather than erroring or moving `revokedAt`, which would claim the connection was live until the second click.

**What survives is the evidence already collected and the fetch log.** Deleting those would rewrite the compliance record. Erasure is a different gesture with a different name: deleting the organisation, which cascades.

`FetchNow` checks this before anything else it does, so "revoking stops future fetches" is an ordering property rather than a promise, and it is asserted by a test that watches the gateway never being reached.

Every attempt, including the ones policy refused. Required scope: `integrations:read`. **Served as of ENT-231.**

**The refusals are the half worth reading.** A log showing only successful fetches is indistinguishable from a deployment where the gateway does nothing, and the customer's question is what Kindlast tried to do rather than only what it managed. `outcome` is `succeeded`, `refused` or `failed`; three rather than two, because a refusal is what a working control produces and not a kind of failure.

`detail` carries the sentence a person reads: "the tool is not granted on this connection" is a policy working, and the console renders it as "Declined" rather than as an error.

`redactions` is how many values were replaced before anything was stored. **Zero is a fact rather than a missing value**: it says the redactor ran and found nothing.

`evidenceId` links a successful fetch to the observation it produced, so "what we fetched" and "what we believe" are one story. Leave `integrationId` empty for the organisation-wide view. Keyset paged over `requestedAt` descending, like every other unbounded listing here; a token is issued only when the page was full.

The live request from the rail: fetch synchronously and store what comes back as evidence. Required scope: `integrations:write`. **Served as of ENT-231.**

**A refusal comes back as a successful RPC carrying a `refused` fetch record**, not as an error, and this is the choice most likely to look wrong at first glance. A refusal returned as an error would show the customer a red box and leave "what we fetched" empty, so they would see a product that failed rather than one that declined. The record is the feature.

**The order of the checks is the behaviour.** Revoked first, because "revoking stops future fetches" is an acceptance criterion and a check placed after the call would satisfy its letter with the fetch already made. Then the tool grant. Then the credential is unsealed. Only then does anything leave, and the gateway checks the egress allow-list and the policy again before it dials.

**Bounded rather than durable.** At build-order step 8 this becomes a Temporal activity with a retry policy and a heartbeat. Temporal is not here, so the bounds are explicit: a context deadline, a capped retry with backoff inside the gateway that never retries a refusal, and exactly one fetch row written per call whatever the outcome. That last part is what will make a replayed activity merely noisy rather than wrong.

The response carries the stored fetch, including `evidenceId` and `redactions`, so a caller can go straight from what it asked for to what was kept.

Where this organisation's model runs, what this deployment permits, and what a person is told before changing it. Required scope: `model:read`. **Served as of ENT-236.**

**Every member may ask this, not only an owner.** "Where does our compliance data get processed" is a question anybody in the organisation may reasonably ask, and a product answering it only for the person who can change it is one nobody else can check.

`setting.hosted` is false for the default state, which is the model this deployment runs itself and where nothing leaves. There is no row for that case and no provider name for it: inventing one would make the absence of a decision look like one.

`permittedProviders` is the operator's list, from `KINDLAST_BYOK_PROVIDERS`. **Empty is the default and it permits nobody**, including an owner, so "nobody at this company may point our compliance data at an external API" is a line in a configuration file rather than a policy every owner has to be trusted to follow. Each entry is a name and the host an endpoint must have; a leading dot makes the host a suffix, for a customer's own subdomain.

`consequenceNotice` and `revertNotice` are served rather than written into a console. There is one copy of each sentence, so a self-hoster's own client shows the same words and neither can drift from what the product does.

`credentialLastFour` is the last four characters of the stored key. **No RPC on this surface returns a key**, so a client could not display one if it wanted to.

Send this organisation's model calls to a hosted provider. Required scope: `model:write`. **Served as of ENT-236.**

**This is a compliance event, not a settings write**, and four things refuse it independently, in this order:

1. The deployment must permit the provider. `failed_precondition` otherwise, and an unconfigured deployment says so rather than saying you are not an owner, which would imply an owner could.
2. The caller must be an **owner**. `permission_denied` otherwise. A role threshold is a decision, so it is checked in Go rather than by a policy.
3. `acknowledgeConsequence` must be true. Without it the call is refused and **the refusal message is the consequence notice itself**, so the only way to make this change is to have been handed the sentence describing it. A client cannot skip the warning by not rendering one.
4. `baseUrl` must be HTTPS, must be on the provider's host, and must resolve to a public address. Private, loopback and link-local answers are refused, and one private answer among several refuses the lot. Checked again on every use, not once here.

**`apiKey` is write only.** It is sealed with the deployment's integration key before it reaches a column, is never returned by any RPC, and never appears in `agent_runs` or a trace. Empty is a real configuration: a provider on the customer's own network may need no bearer token. A deployment with no `KINDLAST_INTEGRATION_KEY` refuses a keyed provider rather than storing it in plaintext.

**Calling this while a provider is already active replaces the row rather than editing it.** The old choice is revoked and a new one inserted, so the sequence of rows is the history of where this customer's data has been processed. The audit entry says `model_provider_enabled`, `model_provider_changed` or `model_provider_rotated` depending on what was there before, because those are three different things to have happened.

`auditEntryId` is the `audit_log` row this produced, so a client can link to the record rather than assert one was made.

item.name: Go back to the bundled model (UseBundledModel)

request.description:
Go back to the model this deployment runs itself. Required scope: `model:write`. **Served as of ENT-236.**

Owner only, and deliberately **no acknowledgement flag**. Stopping data leaving is not a decision anybody needs protecting from, and friction on the safe direction would make the unsafe one look equivalent.

It revokes the active choice and destroys the stored key in the same statement, which a check constraint requires: a revoked row holding a sealed key would be a credential at rest in a system told to stop using it.

**What it cannot do is stated rather than implied.** Content the provider has already processed stays with them, subject to whatever the customer's agreement with that provider says. What bounds the period is the other half of this feature: `agent_runs.provider` records which runs went where, so "everything between these two dates" is answerable.

An organisation already on the bundled model gets a 200 with no `auditEntryId`, and **no audit row is written**. Recording a reversal nobody performed would put a decision nobody made into a regulatory record.

What a machine fetched from a customer's own system. Required scope: `internal:ingest`. **Served as of ENT-231**, on the `kindlast_agent` pool.

**The door evidence comes in by when nobody is signed in**: the scheduled Watcher at build-order step 8, and any gateway-initiated fetch running for an organisation with no session behind it.

**And there is a second door on the core surface, which is deliberate rather than a duplication.** A live fetch a person asked for arrives on a user token, and a user token by design can never carry an `internal:*` scope. Routing it through here would mean either issuing internal scopes to people, which undoes what ENT-207 built, or writing without the person's identity, which loses `requestedBy` on the one record where "which human asked" matters most. So a machine ingests here and a person's fetch goes through `IntegrationsService.FetchNow`. Both write the same two rows; neither is reachable by the other's caller.

**`orgId` is in the body**, for the reason `RecordAgentRun`'s is: this caller holds no session and names its tenant per call. Safe only because `internal:ingest` is issued to service principals through client credentials and never to a browser.

**What this does NOT do**: no egress allow-list, no tool-grant decision, no redaction. All three happened in the gateway before the content crossed the network, and each needs something this process does not hold. **A second redaction pass here would be the worst of them**, because a second implementation is free to disagree with the first and the one that decides what a customer's data looks like has already run.

What it does enforce is the shape: real uuids, an outcome from the closed set, a reason for anything that was not a success, no content on a refusal, and JSON that parses. Send `outcome: "refused"` with a `detail` and no `contentJson` to record a fetch that policy stopped; the response then carries a `fetchId` and an empty `evidenceId`.

item.name: Gateway: what does this endpoint offer (internal)

request.description:
**Served by `apps/workers`, not by core-api**, on `{{gateway_base_url}}`. Required scope: `internal:gateway`. **Served as of ENT-231.**

This is the only service in the repository implemented somewhere other than core-api, and the boundary is the point. core-api holds the database credential and the key that seals third-party credentials; giving it an HTTP client pointed at a URL a customer typed would put request forgery in the process with the most to reach. The gateway holds neither, is handed one fetch at a time, and returns what it found.

**Authentication is a shared secret presented as a bearer token, not an OIDC access token, and that is a deliberate narrowing.** This service has one caller, inside the compose network, with no person and no organisation of its own, so there is nothing for a subject, an audience or a tenancy to mean. A client-credentials round trip would mean core-api acquiring and refreshing an OAuth client it uses for nothing else. The secret is compared in constant time and is mountable from a file. Set `gateway_token` in your environment; the compose default is `gateway-dev-shared-secret-value` and is development-only.

**No published port.** Reachable only on the compose network, which is why this request will not work from a host shell unless you publish one; the secret is defence in depth behind that rather than instead of it.

The endpoint is checked against the egress allow-list **before any packet leaves**: no DNS lookup, no TCP connection, no bytes. The dialer then resolves the name once, refuses if any returned address is private, loopback, link-local or unspecified, and connects to a literal address from that same answer, so a DNS rebind cannot move the target between the check and the connection. Redirects are refused outright, because following one would send the customer's credential to whatever address the response named.

**Served by `apps/workers`**, on `{{gateway_base_url}}`. Required scope: `internal:gateway`. **Served as of ENT-231.**

**The policy travels in the request rather than being looked up here, because the gateway holds no database handle.** That makes the caller responsible for sending the truth and the gateway responsible for refusing anything the policy does not permit, which is the right split: core-api cannot be relied on to be free of bugs, so the gateway checks what it was sent rather than assuming it was filtered.

**`grantedTools` and `writeGrantedTools` are two lists rather than one list with a flag per entry.** With a flag, a caller that forgets to populate it sends a request where every tool reads as read-only and a write goes through on a message that was merely incomplete. With two lists, forgetting the second refuses every write, which is the direction a mistake should fail in.

**Try this request with `writeGrantedTools` emptied.** It comes back `permission_denied` with "close_ticket can change data in that system and this connection has not granted it write access", and nothing was dialled.

**`writeCapable` is the caller's belief and is checked against the endpoint's own annotation**, with the union taken: either side calling it a write makes it a write. That is what catches a tool which has STARTED writing since discovery, where core-api's stored flag is months old and the server's annotation is current.

**The order is egress, then policy, then the rate limit, then the dial.** Every refusal happens with zero bytes on the wire, which is what makes "refused before any request leaves" a property a test can assert rather than a sentence in a document.

**The response is already redacted.** The redactor runs here, before this crosses back, so the process that writes the row never holds the unredacted form and there is no ordering available in which storage happens first. `redactions` counts what it replaced; `fetchedAt` is the gateway's own clock, because a customer's server is free to have a wrong one and `observedAt` has to mean something.

Where this organisation has got to, without starting anything. Required scope: `onboarding:read`. **Served as of ENT-212.**

**A read that creates nothing, deliberately.** Every authenticated route in the console asks this before deciding whether to route a person into onboarding, and a read that quietly opened a session would mean merely LOOKING at the console started an interview. Opening one is `StartOnboarding`.

`profileExists` is the field the console actually gates on, and it is about the compliance profile rather than about a completed session: a profile could arrive another way, and what decides whether the console has anything to show is the profile. **Watch for proto3 field omission when reading it**: an organisation with no profile answers with the flag absent rather than `false`, so a client that treats absent as unknown will never route anybody.

`state.transcript` is the whole conversation, oldest first, ordered by the database's `ordering` column rather than by timestamp: two turns written in one transaction share a transaction timestamp and would tie.

`state.draft` is what WOULD be recorded if the person confirmed now. It is derived from the answers rather than stored, so it cannot drift from them, and each entry carries both the typed value and the verbatim words that produced it. That pairing is the check that makes the profile worth trusting: "we read this as a list of three countries" is checkable and the list alone is not.

An organisation that has never started answers with an empty `sessionId` rather than a `not_found`, because "there is nothing here yet" is the answer the caller is asking for and an error would make every route handle a failure.

Opens the interview, or hands back the one already open. Required scope: `onboarding:write`. **Served as of ENT-212.**

**Idempotent by construction.** An organisation with an unfinished session gets that session back with `created: false`, so a refresh, a second tab and a retry after a dropped connection all land in the same conversation. Two sessions would mean two transcripts and, at confirmation, two profiles.

**It does not re-open a completed interview.** A completed session comes back as it is. Re-interviewing would leave an organisation with two sessions and two profile rows, and the console would have to decide which is real. Changing an answer after onboarding is `MemoryService/CorrectFact`, which keeps the previous value and records who changed it.

The first call also writes the greeting into the transcript, and every call records the next question if it is not already the last turn. **Asking is a write**: the question a person is looking at is a row, so a refresh shows the same conversation rather than a differently worded one.

A brand new organisation is the normal case here. Onboarding is the first thing somebody does after `GetCurrentUser` provisions them, so this has to work against an organisation that holds nothing at all, with no second sign-in.

Answers the question that was asked, or declines it. Required scope: `onboarding:write`. **Served as of ENT-212.**

**`answer` is what the person typed, verbatim, and core-api decides what it means.** The value is parsed into the fact's declared kind at the moment it is given, and an answer that does not fit is refused with `invalid_argument` and a sentence, never interpreted. "About fifty, maybe sixty" is not a staff count and "probably, I think Dave made one" is not an answer about a record of processing activities.

That refusal is the whole design. The profile decides which obligations apply to an organisation, so a field value something inferred produces wrong findings later, far enough from the mistake that nobody traces it back. The legacy flow at `db0bf83` interviewed freely and ran a second model pass over the transcript to extract the profile; this inverts that, and no client should re-implement the parsing, because two implementations of the rule that decides what a customer's profile contains is one too many.

**`skip: true` is not the same as an empty answer.** A skip is a person declining, and it leaves the fact absent from the profile on purpose. A blank `answer` is a mistake and is refused. Collapsing the two would record a deliberate refusal every time somebody submitted too early.

Shapes, from `state.nextQuestion.shape`: `ANSWER_SHAPE_TRI_STATE` accepts exactly `yes`, `no` or `unsure` (unsure is a real answer, and a client offering only two produces a claim nobody made); `ANSWER_SHAPE_NUMBER` accepts a whole number; `ANSWER_SHAPE_LIST` splits on commas, semicolons and newlines but NOT on a bare "and", because "Marks and Spencer" is one company; `ANSWER_SHAPE_TEXT` is kept as typed.

`key` travels in the request rather than being inferred from position, because a person may go back and change an earlier answer, and because a retry must not attach an answer to a different question than the one it was typed under. The latest answer to a key wins and the earlier one stays in the transcript.

Records what was said as what the organisation believes. Required scope: `onboarding:write`. **Served as of ENT-212.**

**The only call in this service that writes a fact.** Until it is made, the interview is a conversation and nothing else: rows in `onboarding_messages`, no fact, no profile row, and therefore nothing any finding can have been reasoned from. That is how "the person sees and confirms the profile before it drives anything" is enforced structurally rather than by a screen somebody could skip.

**Where the answers land, which is the point of ENT-212.** Each one goes into `org_profile_facts` with `source: onboarding` and `recorded_by` set to the person, through the same close-then-insert path a human correction takes. They are then readable and correctable through `MemoryService/ListProfileFacts` and `CorrectFact`, with history. There is no separate onboarding profile: a profile written into a parallel table would be the one part of what Kindlast knows that nobody could correct.

`compliance_profiles` is written too, and it is a **projection rather than a second source of truth**. `run_watcher()` reads that table in plpgsql and knows nothing about the fact store, so until that read moves, a fact write refreshes the projection in the same transaction. `CorrectFact` does the same, which is what makes a correction the thing the next sweep actually reads.

**Idempotent in both the ways that bite.** Confirming twice writes no second profile, because the upsert is keyed on the session. And a fact confirmed at the value it already holds writes no history row, so a double-clicked button and a retried request both leave one profile and one history entry per answer.

Refused with `failed_precondition` when nothing has been answered: a profile of eleven defaults nobody stated would have the Watcher producing findings the customer never gave it grounds for.

Writes the regulatory corpus. Required scope: `internal:ingest`. **Served as of ENT-207.**

**Use the client-credentials token, not a human one.** This is the platform surface: `internal:*` scopes are issued to service clients and never to the browser client, so a console token is refused before any handler runs. `internal:ingest` is the same scope RunSweep carries.

**No organisation header, and that is not an omission.** The corpus has no `org_id`, so there is no organisation for a tenancy interceptor to resolve. This runs on the shorter interceptor chain, like the sweep.

**It takes a pack, and nothing in the contract names GDPR or the AI Act.** A pack is a document with its articles, recitals and annexes, plus obligations, guidelines and enforcement decisions. Every field is optional, so correcting one obligation's severity does not mean re-sending 200KB of unchanged articles. A third regulation is a third call rather than a code change.

**Start with `dryRun: true`.** It validates everything and writes nothing, and it reports every dangling citation at once rather than failing on the first, so a curator can see whether to fix the pack or ingest the regulation it depends on. A real run with an unresolved citation fails with `failed_precondition` instead, because a partially-good pack must not look like a success with a note attached.

**An obligation's `appliesWhen` uses a closed vocabulary, and an unknown token is refused** (ENT-233). The keys are `role`, `requires`, `thresholds`, `engages_processor` and `lawful_basis_includes`; the gap tokens are `ropa`, `dpo`, `ai_register` and `transfer_safeguards`; the thresholds are `cross_border_transfers`, `high_risk_processing`, `high_risk_ai_system` and `large_scale_monitoring`. This is the same class of refusal as a citation that does not resolve, and for the same reason: an unrecognised `requires` token counts as SATISFIED by the Watcher, so the obligation would store cleanly, report as applying, and then never raise a finding, for ever. The message names the token and the vocabulary it is missing from, because whoever hits it is authoring a pack and needs to know whether to add data or add code. `docs/regulation-packs.md` has the reasoning and the boundary.

**Every token in that vocabulary is one the Watcher evaluates** (ENT-246). There is no declared-but-unread tier any more: it held three tokens, and holding them meant Article 35's DPIA obligation reached every controller rather than only high-risk processing, because a condition the evaluator does not recognise narrows nothing. `employees_min` went the other way, evaluated and used by no obligation, and is gone. The three processing-level conditions are answered from `org_profile_facts`, and an organisation that has not answered one is not bound by the obligation that narrows on it. `lawful_basis_includes` takes an Article 6(1) basis and nothing else.

**Idempotent.** Every row upserts on its natural key: a document on CELEX, an article on (document, number), an obligation on slug. Running the same pack twice produces no duplicates and no drift, which matters because §20.3 makes this a scheduled singleton once Temporal lands. An unchanged re-ingest does not even bump `updated_at`, so "what changed last Tuesday" stays answerable.

**One transaction, and nothing is ever deleted.** A pack that fails leaves nothing behind. The `kindlast_ingest` role holds insert and update and no delete grant, because a finding cites an obligation and an obligation cites an article, and removing either out from under a stored finding turns a claim a customer could check into a dangling reference, retroactively.

**Ordering matters when you send several packs**: obligations cite articles, so the regulations go first. A run that sent obligations first would have every one of them refused against an empty corpus, entirely correctly. `data/corpus/packs.json` is where that order is now declared, and adding a regulation is a line in it rather than a code change (ENT-233).

The practical way to load `data/corpus/` is the command rather than this request:

```
go run ./apps/core-api/cmd/corpus-load \
  -api http://localhost:8000 -token "$TOKEN" -dry-run
```

One wire detail that fails silently if you hand-write a pack: proto3 JSON carries **int64 as a string**, so `fineEur` on an enforcement decision must be quoted. `hasFine` rides alongside it because proto3 JSON omits a zero, and a penalty of nothing is a different fact from no penalty.

One agent run: what was asked, what answered, what it consulted, what it cost, how it ended. Required scope: `internal:intelligence`. **Served as of ENT-218.**

**A different scope from its neighbour above, and that is the point rather than an inconsistency.** The scope option is per method precisely so one internal surface can hold writes that different platform callers make: the corpus loader may not record agent runs and Intelligence may not rewrite the law. What they share is that no person's token reaches either. The package answers "is this reachable by a human"; the scope answers "by which of us".

**`orgId` is in the body, not a header, and this is the only write on the platform surface where a caller names its own tenant.** Intelligence holds no session, so it has no active organisation to derive; a run happens for whichever tenant the work belonged to. That is safe only because `internal:intelligence` is issued to one service principal through client credentials and never to a browser client, so "the caller could name any organisation" describes a component we ship rather than an input a person controls. **If that scope ever reaches something a customer can drive, this becomes a tenancy hole.**

**Intelligence does not write this itself** because it holds no database credential (§1.6). Go persists; Python drafts and returns. The record travels back over this RPC, which also means it is written by something that can be trusted to report the org honestly.

**Called once, at the end.** There is no start call to pair with. A record its producer can amend afterwards is worth less than one it cannot, which is the argument `audit_log` rests on, and 00019 enforces it by granting update to nobody at all. The cost is that an in-flight run is invisible until it finishes; `queuedAt` is here from the start so ENT-238's queue wait is a subtraction rather than a migration.

**`AGENT_RUN_OUTCOME_REFUSED` is first class and is not a kind of failure.** §26.3 makes refusal what a working guardrail produces: a budget exhausted, a citation that did not resolve, an em dash the house style forbids, a tool outside the skill's allow-list. An enum with only success and failure would push refusals into one of them and lose the distinction that matters most for trust, which is "the harness stopped this" versus "the harness broke". `AGENT_RUN_OUTCOME_UNSPECIFIED` is refused rather than defaulted, because guessing would put a definite-looking value in the column a customer reads to decide whether to trust a finding.

**`citationsJson` carries both halves, and the rejected half is the important one.** A validator that silently dropped a bad citation would leave a record indistinguishable from a run where the model never tried to cite anything. The customer's question is "what did it get wrong", and an omission cannot answer it. This is not theoretical: asked three times which GDPR article requires a record of processing activities, the 2B tier answered 50, then 34, then 54. The answer is 30, and every response was schema-valid.

**`cachedInputTokens` is separate from `inputTokens`** because every provider offering prompt caching prices it separately, and because with a local model it is the measurement showing the corpus prefix is reused rather than reprocessed.

**`costMicros` is quoted**, being an int64 in proto3 JSON. Zero is the honest value for a local model rather than a missing one.

**Skill and model versions are required and refused when empty.** A run recorded without them answers "what produced this" with "something", which is worse than no row because it looks like an answer. For a local model, `modelVersion` is the weights' digest.

**`onBehalfOfUserId` is checked rather than believed, as of ENT-230.** It used to be written straight to the column, which meant a caller holding `internal:intelligence` could put any person's name on any run, in that person's own organisation's compliance record. Now a run that names somebody must also carry `delegation`, the credential core-api minted while serving that person's own request, and the two must agree; a run carrying no delegation must name nobody, which is what a scheduled sweep does. Both fields are empty in the body above for that reason: this request records a sweep.

**The delegation is EVIDENCE here and AUTHORITY nowhere else on this surface.** On the console requests it travels in the `Kindlast-Delegation` header and the request runs as the person. Recording a run is something the machine does as itself, on a scope no person holds, so it travels in the message instead. `orgId` must match the delegation's organisation too: a delegation is single-org, and a run recorded against another tenant is a caller bug rather than something to resolve silently.

Every refusal here is `permission_denied` with the same message, whether the delegation expired, was revoked, names somebody else or never existed. Four distinguishable answers would make this an oracle for which delegations are live.

The write runs on `kindlast_agent`, which holds insert and select on `agent_runs` and no update or delete. Minimal on purpose: §26.4's versioned profile reference and normalised evidence rows are ENT-228's, and `toolCallsJson` and `citationsJson` are jsonb precisely so that issue can normalise them without these columns changing meaning.

**`provider` (ENT-236).** Who served the run: `instance` for the deployment's own endpoint, otherwise the organisation's chosen provider. `model` and `modelVersion` cannot answer this, because both come from the Intelligence container's environment and are therefore constants of the deployment: an organisation switching provider changes neither, and the run before and the run after read identically. Empty is read as `instance` rather than refused, so an older Intelligence build against a newer core-api records something true rather than nothing. **The provider key is not a field here and never will be**: `agent_runs` is a table a customer exports and hands to somebody else.

The Analyst, as an RPC. Required scope: `internal:intelligence`. **Served as of ENT-218.**

**A DIFFERENT SERVICE FROM EVERYTHING ELSE IN THIS COLLECTION.** This is Python, not core-api, which is why it has its own base URL. §1.6 splits the languages so Go loads and Go persists while Python drafts and returns, and this sits on the far side of that line: it holds no database credential, sets no tenancy GUC, and has no way to write a finding. The one thing it writes, it writes through core-api's `RecordAgentRun`.

**Use the client-credentials token.** No user token reaches this on any path. Two independent things enforce it: the audience is `kindlast-intelligence` and a human's console token carries a different one, and `internal:intelligence` is granted only to the machine user. That is not belt and braces: Intelligence has no tenancy GUCs and no RLS session, so it cannot check whether a human should see what it is processing. It never needs to, because a human cannot reach it.

**THE CALLER PASSES THE OBLIGATIONS, AND THEY ARE THE ONLY ONES THAT MAY BE CITED.** There is no fetch-them-yourself here and the absence is deliberate (§26.2). Inputs are what a skill needs before it starts and there is no decision in fetching them, so the caller assembles them in Go where the corpus is already readable. That keeps a run a pure function of its inputs, which is what makes it activity-shaped for Temporal at step 8.

The validator checks citations against **this list**, not against the corpus, and that is stronger than it sounds. A citation to an obligation that genuinely exists but is not in the list is still a fabrication: the model produced it from somewhere other than its context. Asking the corpus "does this exist" would have accepted it.

**A REFUSAL IS A 200, NOT AN ERROR.** §26.3 makes refusal what a working guardrail produces: a budget exhausted, a citation that did not resolve, a tool outside the allow-list. Returning `internal` for those would tell you the harness broke when it did exactly what it was built to do. Check `outcome`, not the status code.

**A refused narrative is not returned at all**, not even with a warning attached. `AGENTS.md` calls a fabricated citation worse than nothing, and handing a caller prose plus a note is how that prose reaches a customer.

**THE MODEL EXPLAINS APPLICABILITY AND DOES NOT STATE THE LAW, AS OF ENT-248.** The output field is `whyItAppliesToYou`, not `narrative`, and the rename is half the fix: a field called narrative gets a narrative, and a narrative contains whatever the model thinks belongs in one. Two live runs on the 2B tier cited Article 30 correctly and stated Article 30(5) backwards beside it, one asserting the obligation applies to every controller regardless of size and the other reasoning from a missing record to a headcount exemption. The citation validator passed both, correctly. Nothing validated the claim.

The statement of law comes from `summary`, which a person wrote, and `FindingsService` returns it as `citation.obligationSummary` so a client renders it beside the generated prose. If the model is never asked to state the law, it cannot misstate it, and that is a property of the design rather than a probability.

**AND A CLAIM CRITIC REFUSES A DRAFT THAT STATES THE LAW ANYWAY.** A prompt is a request; only code refuses. It matches by named pattern, never by a second model's opinion: an article or recital number, a universal quantifier over legal subjects ("applies to every controller"), "regardless of", the vocabulary of exemptions and thresholds, an instrument as the subject or object of a requirement verb, and a class of legal persons attached to "must". "You must write this down" passes; "controllers must" does not, and the subject is the whole distinction. `outcomeDetail` names the rule that fired and quotes the words around it. It cannot catch a false statement of law that avoids every one of those shapes, and it refuses a TRUE statement of law as readily as a false one, because the product does not need the model to state the law at all.

**`appliesBecause` IS WHY THE OBLIGATION WAS RAISED FOR THIS ORGANISATION, AND IT IS AN INPUT.** Both of the runs above invented their own grounds, because nothing had given them any, and what a 2B invents comes from whatever it remembers about the regulation. core-api renders these from the obligation's stored `applies_when`; it does not re-evaluate them, because the sweep already decided they hold and a second evaluator disagreeing with the first is what produced ENT-246. Optional: omit it and the block is left out of the prompt entirely rather than sent empty, since a model shown an empty list reads it as "no grounds".

**AN EM DASH OR EN DASH IN THE NARRATIVE IS ALSO A REFUSAL, AS OF ENT-163.** `AGENTS.md` forbids both characters in anything a customer reads. The system prompt has asked the model not to use them since ENT-160 and they kept arriving, which is the whole lesson: a prompt is a request, and only code refuses. `outcomeDetail` names the character, its position and the words around it, so a caller can tell this apart from a citation refusal without parsing anything. It refuses rather than substituting a comma, because a silent rewrite would edit a claim about the law with nobody as its author.

**`rejectedCitations` is the field to read when something looks wrong.** A response carrying only the good citations would be indistinguishable from a run where the model never tried to cite anything. This is not theoretical: asked three times which GDPR article requires a record of processing activities, the 2B tier answered 50, then 34, then 54. It is 30, and every answer was schema-valid.

**`agentRunId` is the row in `agent_runs`**, so a finding can point at the record of how it was made. Empty only when recording failed, and that case comes back as an error rather than a success: a narrative whose provenance was never stored is a finding nobody can check.

**`signal` is treated as data and never as instruction.** It reaches the model inside a fenced user message and never in the system prompt, because a compliance profile concatenated into a system prompt is a way to reprogram the Analyst.

**`delegation` is how a run acts for a person without this service ever holding a user token (ENT-230).** Minted by core-api, short lived, single-org, single-user and revocable. Intelligence cannot make one, cannot read inside one and cannot widen one; all it can do is hand it back, on `RecordAgentRun` and in the `Kindlast-Delegation` header of any tool call it makes. That is what keeps a machine principal from being able to act as whoever it names. Empty for a scheduled sweep, and empty here, because the Analyst declares no tools.

**`modelEndpoint` (ENT-236).** Null for an organisation using the model this deployment runs, which is the default and the case where nothing leaves. Set, it names the provider, the endpoint, the model and the API key for THIS RUN only, and core-api is what resolves and checks it: the allow-list and the address check run on every use, so a provider an operator withdraws stops being reachable for organisations that already chose it. Intelligence does no such check and must not be relied on to. It holds the key for the length of one call, never writes it to the run record, and never logs it. A provider that refuses the key **fails the run** and is never quietly answered by the bundled model, because a silent fallback would process a customer's findings somewhere other than where their own record of processing says.

Draft narratives for findings that have none. Required scope: `internal:intelligence`. **Served as of ENT-245.**

**THE HALF ENT-218 ASSUMED AND NOBODY SCHEDULED.** ENT-218 shipped the harness, the guardrail ring, the citation validator and the `agent_runs` record, and nothing in the product called any of it. This is the call.

**A JOB, NOT PART OF THE SWEEP.** A model call inside the sweep's transaction would hold it open for minutes per finding on a local model, block the act path behind its locks, and lose everything on a timeout. The sweep stays fast and deterministic; this runs afterwards over findings that have no narrative. Latency and refusals become a queue's problem rather than a request's, which is also what makes it activity-shaped for Temporal at step 8.

**A NARRATIVE IS ADDED AND NEVER SUBSTITUTED.** It writes `findings.narrative`, `findings.agent_run_id` and `findings.narrative_generated_at`, and touches `detected`, `proposed_action`, `severity` and `status` not at all. The version that overwrote the sweep's text is ENT-164: model prose landed in `detected`, which the feed card renders as a heading, so a short phrase became a paragraph. Adding rather than overwriting means a refused run costs nothing and a deployment with no model is quieter rather than degraded.

**EACH RUN IS OFFERED EXACTLY ONE OBLIGATION: the finding's own.** The validator refuses any citation outside what was offered, so a narrative citing a different article is refused even when that article genuinely exists. This is the check that catches what the local model actually does: asked which GDPR article requires a record of processing activities, the 2B answered 50, then 34, then 54. It is 30. Offering the whole corpus would make that fabrication indistinguishable from a good citation.

**`intelligenceAvailable: false` IS A SUPPORTED ANSWER, NOT AN ERROR.** Intelligence sits behind the `model` compose profile, and `KINDLAST_INTELLIGENCE_URL` defaults to empty. A stack without it still produces findings with their deterministic text. “We have no model” and "the model is broken" want different reactions from an operator, so they are different responses.

**Read all four counts.** `narrated` plus `refused` plus `failed` should equal `attempted`. "3 of 10 narrated" is a different situation from "3 tried and 7 refused", and refusal is the guardrail working (§26.3) rather than a failure. A refusal is recorded on the finding so the next pass does not retry it forever, and so a customer can see that we tried and what was wrong with the answer.

**Runs are sequential.** One `llama-server` serves one request at a time, so firing these concurrently moves the queue rather than shortening it. Expect this to take minutes per finding on a local model.

**core-api NEEDS ITS OWN CREDENTIAL TO SERVE THIS, and the first version had none.** Intelligence declares `internal:intelligence` on `DraftNarrative` and refuses an unauthenticated call, so a core-api that sent no bearer token reported every finding as `failed` with “a bearer token is required”. Set `KINDLAST_INTERNAL_CLIENT_FILE` (the compose stack points it at the same `/machinekey/core-api-client.json` Intelligence reads, so both sides of the call are one credential rather than two that can drift) or `KINDLAST_INTERNAL_CLIENT_ID` and `KINDLAST_INTERNAL_CLIENT_SECRET`. Without it core-api warns at boot and answers `intelligenceAvailable: false`, because a narrator that cannot authenticate is not a degraded one, it is one that fails every call.

**A NARRATIVE THAT STATES THE LAW IS NOW ONE OF THE REFUSALS, AS OF ENT-248.** The first two live narrations of the seeded Article 30 finding both cited the obligation correctly and stated Article 30(5) backwards in the prose beside it, and both were recorded as `SUCCEEDED`. The claim critic refuses that, `narrative_refusal` carries the rule that fired and the words around it, and `agent_runs.refusal` carries the whole rejected text and the machine-readable rule names. The rejected text is deliberately NOT in `outcomeDetail`: that string is what the finding page prints under a heading saying the draft was refused, and a false statement of law must not reach a reader through the page that exists to say it was rejected.

**Measured on the running stack, not assumed.** With the credential set, a seeded Article 30 finding narrated in about 40 seconds on the 2B tier, and `detected`, `proposed_action` and `status` were byte-identical afterwards. Re-measured on 2026-08-18 after ENT-248: four consecutive runs over the same finding gave three narratives that explained the organisation without stating the law and one refusal, the refusal naming `an obligation stated over a class of organisations` on the phrase "the rule that businesses must keep these records".

What was decided, by whom, and when. Required scope: `audit:read`. **Served as of ENT-223.**

**This surface reads `audit_log` and nothing else.** Not traces, not model calls, not anything an observability tool holds (§7.2). That firewall is the product rather than an implementation detail: an auditor is buying a record a regulator can be shown, and a record assembled partly from a vendor's telemetry has completeness that depends on that vendor's retention settings. `audit_log` is append-only by trigger, lives in the customer's own database, and is written in the same transaction as the act it describes.

**Read only, and structurally so.** AuditService has no write RPC and will not get one. The table carries an append-only trigger, `kindlast_app` holds no update or delete grant on it, and the only insert path is bound by policy to the human in the GUC.

**No role gate**, unlike BillingService. Every member sees this, viewers included: a plan and a renewal date are commercial facts about the company, but "who approved this finding" is the shared record of the work these people did together. The organisation boundary is still absolute and supplied by RLS.

**There is no failure dimension and no `level` field**, which is the one real difference from the infrastructure log views this is modelled on. A refused act writes nothing, because the gates are constraints and policies and a refusal aborts the transaction the row would have been written in. Every row here is a thing that happened.

**`filter.until` is EXCLUSIVE.** Pulling January and then February with inclusive bounds returns any boundary row twice, and a duplicated decision in an audit file is a question nobody wants to have to answer. A range whose end is at or before its start is `invalid_argument` rather than swapped or ignored: both of those look like they worked, and in an export the difference is a month of decisions versus all of them.

**`filter.query` does not search `before` and `after`.** Those hold whatever the acted-on row contained, which for a DSAR includes a data subject's name, and a substring search across them would turn the audit log into a search engine over the personal data it exists to account for. It searches the action type, the target table, and the actor's name and email. The payloads are still returned in full: it is the search that stops at the boundary, not the record.

**`actor.actorRole` is the role held AT THE TIME**, snapshotted into the row rather than resolved now. A client that looked it up would relabel a past act every time somebody's role changed. `actor.displayName` and `actor.email` are empty for an actor who has left, and the row is still returned: a log that dropped entries when somebody was offboarded would be defeatable by offboarding somebody.

**`agentRunId` and `actor.kind` are declared and always unpopulated.** `agent_runs` arrives with ENT-218 (§26). They exist now so the day an agent produces an act is a server change rather than a contract change, and so nothing gets written on the assumption that every actor is a human.

Pagination is keyset over `(occurred_at desc, id desc)`. The id tie-break matters more here than in the other registers: an act writes the decision and the record it created in ONE transaction, so both rows share `occurred_at` exactly, and without it a cursor skips a row or repeats one forever. `pageToken` is opaque; `pageSize` defaults to 50 and caps at 200.

`availableActionTypes` lists every action type present in this organisation's log, ignoring the filter, so a console can offer only values that would return something.

The same filtered set, as a file an auditor can attach to a report. Required scope: `audit:read`. **Served as of ENT-223.**

**A separate RPC rather than a flag on the list**, because the two answer different questions. The list answers "what is on this page" and is paged by construction. This answers "everything that matched", and an export that silently stopped at a page boundary is worse than none: the auditor cannot see the truncation, and the file is the artefact that leaves the building.

**Check `truncated` on every response.** It is true when the export hit its 50,000 row cap, and it is the only signal there is: a truncated CSV is a valid CSV that simply stops. `rowCount` says how many rows the file holds. Narrow the range and export again.

**The response is a `oneof` and today it is always `content`.** §7 designs the export as a request returning a signed download URL and §25 leaves synchronous-versus-job open. A synchronous body is right at today's volumes; the shape that grows into a URL is decided now, so the day a customer's log outgrows one response it becomes `download` with no contract break and no second RPC. **The synchronous path is the interim, not the decision.**

`content.data` is base64 over Connect's JSON codec, which is how proto `bytes` travel. Decode it before writing the file.

**The file carries a UTF-8 BOM**, for the unglamorous reason that Excel on Windows otherwise reads UTF-8 as the local code page and mangles every non-ASCII name. The names that get mangled are disproportionately not English ones, and this is a record of who did what.

**Spreadsheet formula injection is defused.** Any cell opening with `= + - @` or a leading tab is prefixed with an apostrophe, OWASP's mitigation. Several columns carry text a user chose (a display name, and the `before`/`after` payloads), the person opening the file is an auditor on a corporate laptop, and spreadsheets evaluate those cells. **This changes the exported bytes deliberately**: the record of truth is `audit_log` in the customer's own database, untouched and append-only, and a rendering that can execute is not a safer record. A parser consuming these files should strip a single leading apostrophe.

**The column order is a contract.** Somebody will point a spreadsheet at column C. Append, never rearrange: `occurred_at, action_type, actor_user_id, actor_name, actor_email, actor_role, finding_id, target_table, target_id, before, after, agent_run_id, audit_id`.

Timestamps are RFC 3339 in UTC, not a friendly local format. This file is read in other timezones and possibly years later, and `14:32` with no offset is a fact nobody can verify.

**`format` may be omitted**, and UNSPECIFIED is accepted as CSV. It is the only format there is, so refusing an unset enum would fail every caller written against the obvious reading of a one-value enum. A second format changes that.

A zero-row export is a real answer and still returns a file with its header row: a completely empty file reads as a broken download.

`web`'s download endpoint, in front of ExportAuditEntries. **Implemented as of ENT-223.**

In the collection because it is one of the halves that will never appear in a proto file: a browser-facing route with its own status codes and its own headers, which is exactly what this collection is the source of truth for.

**Authenticated by the session cookie, not a bearer token**, so this request only works from a browser that has signed in. There is nothing to paste into Postman here; it is documented so the contract is reviewable.

**A route handler rather than a server action**, because the result is a file and a download has to survive being a plain link. A server action returning bytes needs client-side JavaScript to turn them into a saved file, and the artefact an auditor's whole workflow ends in should not depend on a hydration step.

It reads the SAME query string the page does, through the same `toFilter`, which is what makes "export what I am looking at" true by construction rather than because two implementations agree. `page` is deliberately dropped: an export is the whole matching set, and carrying a cursor into it would be asking for "everything, starting from page three".

**The filename carries the truncation.** When core-api reports the cap was hit, the file is named `-partial`. That is the only signal that survives the trip: the file gets attached to a report and emailed onwards long after any banner in the console is gone, and a name is the one piece of context that travels with it. `X-Kindlast-Truncated` and `X-Kindlast-Row-Count` carry the same facts for a script.

Status codes worth knowing: **401** with no session, and deliberately not a redirect, because redirecting a file endpoint into a sign-in page saves an HTML document called `audit.csv`. **404** for a slug the caller does not belong to, matching the rest of the console, so this cannot be used to discover which organisations exist. **400** when core-api refused the filter (a backwards range). **502** when core-api was unreachable or returned no file; a response with no content is a fault rather than an empty export, because an export of nothing still carries a header row and a zero-byte file looks like an answer.

`Cache-Control: no-store, private`. This is a per-organisation record behind a session, and a shared proxy holding one tenant's audit log is the worst cache bug available in this product.
